hypothesis.hypothesis:
Make the front end decoupled (structural change of the IF/ID boundary),
and use the same restructure to take the hazard terms off the PC enable.
Cut cone B in the same change, because the LESSONS show tied cones must
go together.

1. Prefetch queue (if_stage.sv, new rtl/fetch_queue.sv or inline):
   - Add a 2-entry FIFO of {pc, instr} between the imem and ID, with a
     registered count and a head pointer. Store pc per entry; do not
     re-add pc+4 on the ID path.
   - ID input bundle = count_q != 0 ? head entry
                                    : {fetch_pc, imem_data, valid = imem_ready}.
     This bypass keeps redirect -> target -> ID at today's latency, so
     the taken-branch penalty stays 2 cycles. The select is a single
     flop and both data inputs are flops on the bench (lfsr / queue),
     so the ID cone gains exactly one LUT.
   - Fetch enable is REGISTERED-ONLY: fetch_go = count_q != 2. PC
     advances (pc <= pc + 4) when imem_ready && fetch_go. Redirect is
     last: pc_d = redirect ? redirect_target : pc_seq, where pc_seq
     (pc or pc + 4) is computed from imem_ready and count_q, with no
     load_use / dmem_stall / ex_busy terms. Drop the CE-style enable and
     use a plain D mux with redirect as the final 2:1 level. The
     redirect -> pc path becomes compare -> taken -> 1 mux LUT.
   - Push when the fetch succeeded AND (the queue is non-empty OR ID
     does not consume this cycle). Pop when ID consumes
     (!stall_id && count_q != 0). ID "consumes" = the ID/EX register
     captures (!stall_id). These enables feed only the queue flops.
   - On redirect, flush the queue (count <= 0). The wrong-path slots in
     the queue die exactly like today's IF slot, and flush_id still
     kills the ID/EX wrong-path slot.
   - hazard_unit: stall_if disappears from the PC path. load_use,
     dmem_stall and ex_busy now only stall ID/EX and the queue pop. The
     NOP/valid=0 on imem stall applies only in the bypass case
     (count_q == 0 && !imem_ready).
   - Liveness: fetch_go only depends on count_q, and count_q drains
     whenever ID consumes, so there is no deadlock. ID/EX hold or bubble
     semantics are unchanged, so the forward-exactness argument in
     forward_unit.sv still holds.
2. Cone A tail (ex_stage.sv, id_stage.sv, core_pkg.sv):
   - Decode the branch condition in ID into registered one-hots
     br_eq, br_lt and br_inv, plus registered 33-bit compare-extension
     bits (sign for BLT/BGE, 0 for BLTU/BGEU), folded into the bit-31
     forward LUT like mul_a_sx.
   - EX then does one 33-bit subtract whose carry-out is lt.
     taken = ((br_eq & eq) | (br_lt & lt)) ^ br_inv, gated by a
     registered is_branch.
   - Precompute the branch and JAL misalign bits in ID (pc[1:0] is
     always 00 here, so the misalign bit is just imm[1]) as flops. Only
     JALR still uses agu_sum[1:0], which are early carry bits.
3. Cone B (id_stage.sv, ex_stage.sv, alu.sv):
   - Register a dedicated ALU b-operand in ID:
     alu_b_q = (alu_src ? imm : rs2_fwd) ^ {32{sub}}, with ex_result
     still at the last forward level. The select side (sel2_ex &
     !alu_src, sub) is flop- or IF-derived, so the forward LUT stays
     one level: {sel, ex_result, early_or_imm, sub}.
   - The EX adder is then flop -> carry chain -> AND-OR, which removes
     the alu_b mux and the b-XOR LUT from paths 8 and 21.
   - Also register the 5-bit shift amount pre-muxed (imm[4:0] vs
     rs2_fwd[4:0]).
   - rs2_val stays for stores, the branch compare, MUL and RVFI.
Expected cycles: backend stall episodes are ~40-50k cycles/iteration
(dmem stalls + load/mul-use bubbles). The queue banks ~0.78 of those
fetch slots, capped by depth. About 60% of banked entries are consumed
before a taken-branch flush, hiding one imem bubble each. That is
about 15-20k of ~453k cycles per iteration (-3.5 to -4.5%).
Expected Fmax: cone A loses 3-4 LUT levels after the carry, and cone B
loses 1-2 LUT levels on the adder branch. The shifter branch keeps its
lane but loses the alu_b mux on the shamt side. From ~10.2 ns to
~9.6-9.8 ns data delay gives +4-6%. Combined: about +8%.
Area: +128 FF and ~+90 LUT for the queue, and +33 FF for alu_b_q,
which is well under r3s2's +385 LUT that caused placement pressure.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r5s1 (regression, -7.94%): The bypassed 2-entry prefetch queue cut cycles as forecast (4.37M vs 4.53M, -3.5%), and the one-LUT redirect plus pre-muxed alu_b took the branch -> PC cone out of the top paths, but median Fmax fell from 106.5 to 94.7 MHz (+111 LUT); the most likely cause is that the queue-empty bypass put the raw io_imemReady input and a head/bypass mux level in front of the whole ID cone (instr select -> decoder/imm_gen -> pc+imm -> pre_result, and -> forward selects -> rs2_val), which became a new ~10.1 ns cone tied with the shamt -> shifter -> ex_result -> forward loop, and the implementer's place_option 0 check (98.33 vs 97.65 MHz, +0.7%) did not show the loss, so a decoupled front end should keep imem_ready off the instr/decode bits (let it gate only the ID/EX valid and side-effect ctrl bits, as in r2s0's narrow flush), and Fmax should be compared with the champion's median across placement options, not with option 0 alone.

title: Decode predictor (JAL + BTFN-agree LUT-RAM) paired with a REGISTERED 2-cycle mispredict redirect, taking the EX branch-compare -> PC/flush path off the critical path
motivation:
The champion (hyp-001-r4s0: 235.32 iter/s, 106.5 MHz median, 4,527,646
cycles) has its critical path at ID/EX.rs2_val_0 -> 32-bit branch
compare -> branch_taken -> redirect -> u_if/pc (15.53 ns arrival, about
10.2 ns of data after the 5.33 ns clock insertion, 37 cells). The same
combinational redirect also drives flush_id into the ID/EX ctrl/valid
flops. That path is about one LUT shorter, so the two form a tied cone.
Every taken branch, JAL and JALR costs 1 bubble. The ISS count is
295,904 + 49,629 + 13,794 = 359k bubbles, about 8% of cycles.
The r3s2 and r4s2 decode predictor removed 294k of those cycles
(4.49M -> 4.20M, measured twice). That leaves about 65k penalty events:
13.8k JALRs plus about 51k direction mispredicts. r4s2 kept a
combinational redirect at the last next-PC level, so on r4s0 it could
only win IPC, and it would still leave the champion's critical path
in place.
Once 82% of redirects are gone, the redirect no longer needs to be
fast. A 2-cycle registered mispredict costs only +65k cycles, and it
removes the branch compare from every path into the PC and the ID/EX
flush.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebase r4s2's low-area decode predictor onto r4s0. Make the EX
mispredict redirect REGISTERED, so the EX branch/jump resolution
ends at two flops (redirect_q, target_q) and feeds no PC mux and no
flush.

1. Predictor (new rtl/branch_pred.sv, same as r4s2). It works from the
   IF/ID word (io_imemData, which is an LFSR flop in the timed bench)
   and the pc:
     is_jal = opcode==1101111
     is_br  = opcode==1100011 && funct3 not in {2,3}
     tgt_ok = (is_jal ? instr[21] : instr[8]) == 0   // imm[1]==0
     ctr    = tbl[pc[8:2]]    // 128x2b distributed LUT-RAM, async
                              // read, one sync write port, no reset
     pred   = if_valid && tgt_ok && (is_jal || (is_br && (instr[31] ^ ctr[1])))
   The table trains only from EX/MEM flops: valid && ctrl.is_branch &&
   !is_illegal, at its pc[8:2], using branch_taken, instr[31] and the
   carried ctr, with a saturating update of the agree bit. Its contents
   never affect correctness.
2. IF next PC. pc_imm is the existing id_stage pc+imm adder, so no new
   adder is needed:
     if (redirect_q)  pc <= target_q;              // flop select, top priority
     else if (!stall) pc <= pred ? pc_imm : pc + 4;
   The comb `redirect` / `redirect_target` inputs are removed from
   if_stage.
3. EX mispredict. pred_q is latched into ID/EX and cleared on flush.
   pc4 = ID/EX.pre_result, which is pc+4 for branches.
     mis_br  = is_branch && (pred_q ? !cond : (cond && !misalign_branch))
     mis_jal = is_jump && !is_jalr && !pred_q && !misalign_jump
     mis_jr  = is_jalr && !misalign_jump
     mispredict = (mis_br || mis_jal || mis_jr) && !redirect_q
     tgt = is_jalr ? {agu[31:1],0} : (pred_q ? pre_result : branch_target)
   Registered on every cycle:
     redirect_q <= !reset && mispredict && !dmem_stall  // branch actually leaves EX
     target_q   <= tgt
   A BRANCH/JAL(R) is never a memory op. So in the redirect_q cycle
   EX/MEM holds that branch, dmem_stall is 0, and nothing can hold the
   kill.
4. Wrong-path kill. There are exactly 2 slots, and both use flop
   controls only.
   - The instruction in EX during the redirect_q cycle: EX/MEM captures
     valid=0 and clears reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, is_branch,
     is_jump and is_illegal. It cannot set redirect_q (the !redirect_q
     term), cannot touch dmem (no oob), and cannot train. If it is a
     DIV, flush_id removes it and the divider FSM returns to IDLE on
     !req. Its ex_w_en forward only reaches the ID/EX slot being
     flushed.
   - The IF/ID slot during the redirect_q cycle: flush_id =
     redirect_q || (load_use && !dmem_stall).
   - hazard_unit loses its `redirect` input. PC priority is redirect_q
     over every stall.
   RVFI is unchanged. EX/MEM.pc_next and the trap/reg_write semantics
   stay the resolved outcome computed exactly as today. Killed slots
   never retire, so pc_rdata stays equal to the previous pc_wdata.
Cycle forecast, from the ISS and r4s2's measured counts rebased on
r4s0: 4,527,646 - 294,049 + 65,278 (one extra bubble per remaining
mispredict) = about 4.30M, -5.0%.
Timing basis: `make timing` on r4s0, place_option 0, 97.65 MHz. The
top 25 setup paths are tied within 0.13 ns of data delay:
  (i)   rs2_val_0 -> 32-bit compare carry -> 5 LUTs -> u_if/pc CE, 10.20 ns
  (ii)  the same compare -> ID/EX ctrl/sel RESET (flush_id), 10.09 ns
  (iii) the ALU shift/add lane -> 4-LUT one-hot result -> rs?_fwd ->
        ID/EX rs?_val / mul_a_sx, 10.12-10.16 ns (about 60% routing)
This change removes (i) and (ii). The branch compare, JALR AGU and
target now end at redirect_q/target_q, and the pred_q XOR lives only
in that flop cone. Nothing new is added to (iii): EX/MEM.alu_result,
ex_result and ex_w_en are NOT gated by the kill, which only touches
valid/ctrl flops. The fetch path (LFSR flop -> imm_gen -> 32-bit
pc+imm carry -> pred mux -> pc D) is estimated at about 6.5-7.5 ns,
well under 10.1 ns. Fmax should therefore stay about flat, capped by
(iii) at about 106 MHz median, or gain 0-2% from removing two tied
cones and relieving the placer. A 1-cycle-penalty port of r4s2 would
instead put the pred_q XOR into (i) and (ii), where each extra LUT is
about -4% Fmax.
Expected fitness: 235.32 x 4.528/4.299 x (1.00..1.02) = about 248-253,
+5-7.5%. The design also composes with any sibling that cuts (iii):
once branch -> PC is off the table, the next limiter would sit
entirely in the ALU loop. Area is about +150 LUT / +45 FF (r4s2
measured +143 LUT and cost about 1% Fmax).

changes.description: New module, as in r4s2. It pre-decodes JAL and valid BRANCH from the IF/ID word and computes the imm[1]==0 target-alignment check. It holds a 128x2-bit agree-with-BTFN counter table in distributed LUT-RAM (async read at pc[8:2], one sync write port, zero init, no reset). pred is gated by the IF slot's valid. It outputs pred and ctr[1:0]. The write port is driven from EX/MEM flops (valid && is_branch && !is_illegal, branch_taken, instr[31], pc[8:2], carried ctr) with a saturating update. If Gowin refuses LUT-RAM inference, fall back to 64 entries at pc[7:2].

Remove the combinational redirect/redirect_target inputs. The new inputs are redirect_q and target_q (flops from ex_stage) plus pred and pc_imm. PC update: redirect_q ? target_q : (!stall ? (pred ? pc_imm : pc+4) : pc). The IF/ID payload is unchanged (NOP on imem stall only).
Export the existing pc_imm (pc + imm) to if_stage, with no new adder. Latch pred_q and ctr[1:0] into ID/EX on !stall. Clear pred_q on flush/reset together with ctrl/valid.
id_ex_t: add pred_q and ctr[1:0]. ex_mem_t: add ctr[1:0] for predictor training.

Replace the combinational redirect outputs with registered redirect_q and target_q. The mispredict terms are: branch direction versus pred_q, unpredicted aligned JAL, and aligned JALR, all AND !redirect_q. redirect_q <= mispredict && !stall (dmem_stall). target_q <= is_jalr ? agu : (pred_q ? pre_result(pc+4) : branch_target). A new kill = redirect_q gates EX/MEM valid, reg_write, mem_read, mem_write, is_branch, is_jump and is_illegal for the wrong-path instruction in EX. pc_next, the misalign trap, ex_w_en and the other RVFI-feeding fields are unchanged.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r5s2 (regression, +2.76%): Rebasing r4s2's low-area decode predictor (JAL + BTFN-agree 128x2 LUT-RAM, predicted target from id_stage's pc+imm) onto r4s0 with a registered 2-cycle mispredict redirect (redirect_q/target_q flops as the top PC priority, the wrong-path EX slot killed through valid/ctrl-only EX/MEM clears, flush_id = redirect_q || load_use) scored 241.82, the best entry of round 5 but only about half its +5-7.5% forecast; if cycles reached the forecast ~4.30M, this implies about 104 MHz, ~2% below r4s0's 106.5 MHz median, so taking the branch compare off the paths into u_if/pc and flush_id gained no Fmax (as in r5s0, which also cut that cone and reached only ~108 MHz), most likely because the ALU/shift -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop still caps the clock, while the ~+150 LUT predictor, or its new LFSR -> imm_gen -> pc+imm -> pred mux -> pc fetch path, cost the same ~1-2% that r4s2 paid; the predictor's gain should therefore be counted as IPC only, net of ~2% Fmax, and stacked on a core that shortens the ALU loop rather than justified by removing the branch cone.

title: Cut all four tied cones at once: 2-LUT branch resolve, 3-level shifter, 1-LUT5 ex_result, imem_ready off the ID read path
motivation:
A fresh Gowin report on the r4s0 champion (place_option 0, 97.65 MHz,
10.2 ns data path) shows its top 25 paths tied within 0.1 ns across three
cones:
  (a) rs2_val -> 32-bit compare carry chain (ends at +3.6 ns) -> FIVE LUTs
      in u_if (n328_s7/s6/s5/s3/s0 = branch_op case -> branch_taken ->
      misalign_fault -> redirect -> redirect|!stall) -> pc_30_s3 (fanout 30)
      -> pc CE. The same chain also feeds flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl
      (paths 23-25).
  (b) rs1_val (fanout 14, 2.8 ns route) -> shifter n1_s96 -> n1_s79 ->
      ex_result_*_s11 -> _s6 -> _s2 -> _s0 -> rs1_fwd -> rs1_val: seven LUT
      levels for SLL/SRL/SRA plus the lane merge. alu_src -> alu_b
      (fanout 71) -> shifter is tied with it (path 21).
  (c) sub (fanout 33) -> adder carry -> ex_result -> forward -> mul_a_sx
      (one LUT deeper than rs1_val, because the MUL sign bit is built on
      rs1_fwd[31]).
r5s0 cut (a), (c) and part of (b) and reached only ~108 MHz. Its new worst
path was a fourth cone, (d) stall_gen/imem_ready -> the IF NOP mux
(instr = flush ? NOP : imem_data) -> regfile LUT-RAM address -> x0 zero ->
forward -> rs1_val, at about 9.5 ns. The lessons say tied cones have to be
cut in the same iteration. This entry cuts all four, with no change to the
cycle count apart from a rare DIV-use bubble.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Four cycle-neutral micro-cuts. Each removes 2-3 LUT levels from its cone.
1. Branch/jump resolve down to <=2 LUTs after the carry chain, then the PC
   D mux. In ID, register the operand-independent terms: br_ok = is_branch
   && (pc+imm)[1:0]==0, jal_ok = JAL && target aligned, cmp_use_lt
   (BLT/BGE/BLTU/BGEU), cmp_inv (BNE/BGE/BGEU) and cmp_signed. In EX, lt
   comes from one 33-bit subtract whose extension bits are cmp_signed &
   rs?[31]; eq comes from a separate equality chain. Then
   cond = cmp_use_lt ? lt^inv : eq^inv (LUT4) and
   redirect = jal_ok | jalr_ok | (br_ok & cond) (LUT4). jalr_ok needs only
   agu_sum[1], a 2-bit carry that finishes early. The misalign trap bits for
   EX/MEM ctrl are computed off this path, from the same flops.
   Replace pc's CE (redirect | !stall) with a D mux:
   pc_d = redirect ? redirect_target : pc_seq, where
   pc_seq = stall_if ? pc : pc+4 is computed early. The redirect_target
   mux (is_jalr ? {agu_sum[31:1],0} : branch_target) runs in parallel with
   the compare. flush_id = redirect | early_flush, where early_flush
   (load_use, imem-stall bubble, see 4) is computed from flops and instr
   bits and stays gated by !dmem_stall.
2. An explicit 3-stage shifter in place of the inferred one. Separate SLL
   and SRL/SRA shifters, each stage A = 4:1 by shamt[1:0], stage B = 4:1 by
   shamt[3:2], stage C = 2:1 by shamt[4] fused with the lane select
   (sel_sll / sel_sr, arith fill). The Gowin MUX2_LUT5 makes each 4:1 about
   one LUT level. alu_b stays out of the shift-amount path: for OP-IMM, ID
   writes imm into rs2_val (as in r5s0), and ID/EX keeps a separate
   store/branch rs2 copy only where needed (store data, branch compare).
   That removes the fanout-71 alu_b mux from every lane.
3. ex_result as a single LUT5 per bit after the lanes:
   ex_result = (sum & sel_add) | logic_pre | sll_g | sr_g, where logic_pre
   is one LUT from flops (a, b, lop, and pre_result that ID has already
   ANDed with sel_pre) and slt ORs into bit 0 only. DIV/REM leave
   ex_result: the divider's quo_q is ORed into MEM's alu_or_mul the way the
   MUL product is, and is_div joins ID/EX.late_result (DIV-use bubble,
   almost absent in CoreMark's timed region). The MUL sign-extension bits
   are built in EX from the ID/EX flops (mul_sa & rs1[31], mul_sb & rs2[31])
   in front of the DSP. That takes the extra LUT off the rs1_fwd[31]
   forward output (cone c), and the mul_a_sx/mul_b_sx ID/EX fields are
   deleted.
4. imem_ready off the instruction bits. if_stage passes imem_data to
   ID unmuxed, so no NOP substitution happens. The regfile read addresses,
   decoder, imm_gen and forward compares see raw instr bits straight from
   the fetch flops. The imem-stall bubble becomes a narrow flush: it joins
   flush_id as (imem_stall && !ex_busy), so it clears only ID/EX
   valid/ctrl/lane selects. It never touches the data fields and stays
   gated by !dmem_stall as now. A spurious load_use computed from a
   garbage instr during an imem stall only holds ID/EX data that is
   bubbled anyway, and PC already holds on imem_stall. Also fold the regfile's
   x0 zeroing into the forward select code. forward_unit emits a 2-bit code
   per operand (rf / mem / wb / zero), computed from instr bits in parallel
   with the LUT-RAM read, so rf data -> LUT5 early mux -> LUT5 last-level
   mux (ex_result / load_data / early) -> flop. reg_file becomes a plain
   array read with no compare.
Expected result: cone (a) about 7.5 ns, (b) about 8.3 ns, (c) about 8 ns,
(d) about 8.5 ns, against 10.2 ns now. If no fifth cone sits close behind,
median Fmax should land around 113-116 MHz vs 106.5 at unchanged
cycles (4.53M; the DIV-use bubble should be negligible). That is roughly
+6-9%. The implementer should run `make timing` with --all-options after
each of the four cuts, compare with the champion's median rather than
option 0 (lesson r5s1), and check the top-25 list for any cone not
listed here (candidates: load extract -> forward, EX/MEM -> dmem
address/BSRAM).

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r6s0 (regression, +1.26%): Cutting all four tied cones in one change was forecast at +6-9% but scored 238.28, level with r5s0's 238.68 (about 108 MHz at ~4.53M cycles). The cuts were a 2-LUT branch resolve into a pc_d mux, an explicit 4:1/4:1/2:1 shifter with separate SLL and SR lanes, a one-LUT5 ex_result with DIV behind the late-result interlock, and imem_ready moved off the instr/regfile-address bits with x0 folded into the forward select code. Two rounds that each cut every reported cone by 2-3 LUT levels have now stalled at the same ~108 MHz, inside the ~4-9% place_option spread, so counting LUT levels per cone no longer predicts Fmax on this core. The remaining limit is most likely route delay on high-fanout flops (rs1_val fanout 14 with a ~2.8 ns route, sub fanout 33) and the carry chains in the single-cycle EX -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop, not logic depth. The next Fmax step therefore needs a structural change, such as duplicating the high-fanout operand flops or breaking the forward loop with an ALU-use bubble, or else a timing report on r6s0 that shows a new limiter.

title: Decoupled front end v2: shift-register fetch queue whose flop-selected head replaces the NOP mux (imem_ready only on valid), registered-only PC enable, one-LUT5 ALU merge
motivation:
Two measured facts point the same way.
1. Cycles. r5s1's bypassed 2-entry prefetch queue cut CoreMark cycles
   from 4.53M to 4.37M (-3.5%). Today IF is lock-stepped with ID, so
   every backend stall cycle (dmem stall on ~22% of memory ops,
   load/mul-use bubble, divider) throws away a ready fetch slot, and
   every later imem-not-ready cycle then injects a NOP bubble.
   r5s1 still lost, because its median Fmax fell from 106.5 to 94.7 MHz.
   Its critical path started at stall_gen/imem_ready_s0 and ran through
   u_decoder -> u_imm -> pre_result. The bypass-case instruction was
   `count_q ? head : (imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP)`, which put the raw
   ready input and one extra mux level in front of the whole ID cone.
2. Fmax. r5s0 cut the champion's three tied cones: branch -> PC,
   the ALU -> ex_result -> forward loop, and adder -> MUL sign. It then
   reached ~108 MHz, and its new worst path was
   stall_gen/imem_ready_s0 -> u_if (NOP mux) -> u_rf (LUT-RAM read
   address) -> u_id forward -> rs1_val, 8 cells, ~9.5 ns data.
   The champion has the same NOP mux, driven by flush_if = !imem_ready,
   on its instr bits.
So imem_ready on the instruction bits is now both the Fmax limiter
behind the old cones and the reason the queue's IPC gain was lost.
The NOP mux is not needed: a bubble's data fields are never observed.
Only valid and the side-effect ctrl bits have to die, and ID/EX
already clears exactly those through its narrow flush (r2s0).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild the IF/ID boundary as a decoupled front end in which imem_ready
never touches an instruction bit. Cut the two remaining tied EX-side
cones in the same change, because the LESSONS show tied cones must go
together.

1. Fetch queue (if_stage.sv):
   - A 2-entry SHIFT-REGISTER queue of {pc, instr}. The head is always
     q0, so there is no read-pointer mux. Registered q_cnt (0..2) plus
     one-hot copies q_ne_q (q_cnt != 0) and q_full_q (q_cnt == 2), each
     duplicated as needed so the head-select flop has low fanout.
   - ID input: instr = q_ne_q ? q0.instr : imem_data and
     pc = q_ne_q ? q0.pc : fetch_pc. This is one flop-selected 2:1 LUT.
     It REPLACES today's `imem_stall ? NOP : imem_data` LUT, so the
     fetch -> decoder/imm/regfile -> forward cones keep their current
     depth and lose the imem_ready routing.
     valid = q_ne_q | imem_ready. No NOP is forced anywhere.
   - PC: pc_d = redirect ? redirect_target : pc_seq. pc_seq =
     (imem_ready && !q_full_q) ? pc + 4 : pc, a flop-only term.
     Redirect sits at the last 2:1 level. load_use, dmem_stall and
     ex_busy leave the PC path entirely, which removes the
     `redirect || !stall_if` CE LUT (fanout 30) from the branch -> PC
     cone. There is no clock-enable on pc; it is a plain D mux.
   - Push: the fetch succeeded (imem_ready && !q_full_q && !redirect)
     and NOT (queue empty && ID consumes this cycle). Pop when ID
     consumes (id_take = !stall_id && q_ne_q). Shift q1 -> q0 on pop.
     On redirect, clear q_cnt/q_ne_q/q_full_q. Wrong-path entries die
     like today's IF slot, and flush_id still kills the ID/EX
     wrong-path slot.
2. ID/EX gating (id_stage.sv, hazard_unit.sv):
   - flush_id = (load_use || redirect || !in.valid) && !dmem_stall, so
     a bubble clears only valid/ctrl/lane selects through the existing
     sync-reset. The data fields still capture on !stall alone. Only
     the flop-sourced imem_ready and q_ne_q enter that term.
   - A spurious load_use computed on garbage instr bits of an invalid
     slot is harmless: it bubbles a slot that is already a bubble, and
     nothing is popped (q_ne_q = 0).
   - stall_if disappears. stall_id = dmem_stall || load_use || ex_busy
     now gates only the ID/EX hold and the queue pop.
   - The forward-exactness argument is unchanged. ID/EX, EX/MEM and
     MEM/WB still capture on the same cycles.
3. ALU loop (alu.sv, ex_stage.sv, id_stage.sv), the cone tied with the
   fetch cone in r5s1 (shamt -> shifter -> ex_result -> forward):
   - Gate the SLL/SR lanes inside their last shift-mux level so the
     per-bit ex_result merge is one LUT5:
     (sum & sel_add) | logic_g | sll_g | sr_g | slt.
   - Forward pre_result (LUI/AUIPC/link) from its ID/EX flop at the
     early forward level (sel?_pre). OR pre_result and div_result into
     EX/MEM.alu_result on the D side only, not into ex_result. DIV
     joins late_result, so a DIV-use costs one bubble; CoreMark's timed
     region almost never divides.
   - Build MUL sign bits in EX from rs1_val[31]/rs2_val[31] plus the
     registered mul_sa/mul_sb, so no extra LUT sits behind rs1_fwd[31].
Liveness: the fetch enable depends only on q_full_q, and the queue
drains whenever ID consumes, so there is no deadlock. Redirect always
wins at the PC.

Expected cycles: -3.5% (r5s1 measured 4.37M vs 4.53M with the same
2-entry queue), plus ~+0.1% for DIV-use.
Expected Fmax: the imem_ready -> instr cone is gone. The fetch cone
keeps one mux LUT, now driven by a local, low-fanout flop. The
branch -> PC tail loses the CE LUT. The ALU loop loses 2-3 merge
levels. From the champion's 106.5 MHz median, +2-5%, bounded by
r5s0's ~108 MHz for similar EX cuts.
Combined: about +6%.

title: Short-fetch-path decode predictor: r5s2 policy, raw IF word (imem_ready only in ID/EX flush), 1-LUT pc-relative imm
motivation:
r5s2 moved r4s2's decode-time predictor (JAL plus a BTFN-agree 128x2
LUT-RAM) onto r4s0 with a registered 2-cycle mispredict redirect. It
measured 4,295,423 cycles, 5.1% fewer than r4s0's 4,527,646. That is
the only large cycle cut still on the table. It scored only +2.76%
(241.82) because median Fmax fell from 106.5 to 103.9 MHz.
Its reported worst path is the predictor's own fetch path:
  lfsr (io_imemData) -> u_id/u_imm -> pc+imm carry -> pred mux -> u_if/pc
(21 cells).
The r5s0 and r5s1 worst paths show that the same prefix also caps the
base core:
  r5s0 (108 MHz): stall_gen/imem_ready -> u_if NOP mux -> u_rf read address -> rs1_val
  r5s1:           imem_ready -> u_id/u_decoder -> u_imm -> pre_result
So two things sit in front of every IF-word cone: the `flush ? NOP :
imem_data` mux on io_imemReady, and imm_gen's full 7-bit-opcode case.
In r5s2 the predictor adds a 32-bit carry chain and a PC mux on top of
that prefix, and it becomes the limiter.
If this prefix is cut, the predictor's fetch path ends well below the
~10.1 ns ALU -> ex_result -> forward loop. That leaves r5s2's cycle cut
(-5.1%) at roughly r4s0/r5s0 Fmax (106-108 MHz), which gives about
247-251 iter/s (+5-7%).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Re-implement r5s2's predictor policy exactly as it measured, so the
cycle count stays at about 4.30M. Restructure its front end so that
neither io_imemReady nor the full imm_gen sits on any IF-word cone.

A. Predictor. Same policy as r5s2, in a new rtl/branch_pred.sv.
   - Decode from the IF word: is_jal, a valid is_br (funct3 not 2/3),
     and tgt_ok = imm[1]==0.
   - ctr = tbl[pc[8:2]]: a 128x2 distributed LUT-RAM with async read
     from the PC flop, one sync write port, zero init, no reset.
   - pred = tgt_ok && (is_jal || (is_br && (instr[31] ^ ctr[1]))).
   - Train only from EX/MEM flops (valid && is_branch && !is_illegal,
     branch_taken, instr[31], carried ctr), with the same saturating
     update as r5s2.
   - Mispredicts use r5s2's registered redirect: redirect_q/target_q
     are flops and the top PC priority. The wrong-path EX slot is
     killed through valid/ctrl-only EX/MEM clears, and flush_id takes
     redirect_q. JALR always redirects.
   - pred does NOT need to be gated by imem_ready. On an imem stall
     the PC holds anyway (stall_if), and the slot is bubbled in ID/EX,
     which also clears pred_q.

B. Raw IF word (removes io_imemReady from every decode cone). if_stage
   drives out.instr = io_imemData unconditionally, with
   out.valid = imem_ready.
   - The imem-stall bubble moves to the ID/EX valid/ctrl/sel flush:
       flush_id = redirect_q
                || ((load_use || imem_stall) && !dmem_stall && !ex_busy)
     The !ex_busy term is required. Otherwise a DIV held in ID/EX
     would be flushed during an imem stall.
   - Garbage rs1/rs2 during a stall can at worst raise a spurious
     load_use. That only holds the PC and bubbles ID/EX, which the
     stall does anyway.
   - ID/EX data fields may capture garbage. This is already allowed
     for bubbles: rd is only observed through the flushed
     reg_write/late_result bits.
   - io_imemReady now reaches only the PC clock-enable and the ID/EX
     flush/valid flops, each 1-2 LUTs from the stall-generator flop.

C. 1-LUT pc-relative immediate. The pc_imm adder is used only by the
   branch/JAL target (ID/EX.branch_target and the predicted PC) and by
   the AUIPC pre_result. Feed it a dedicated immediate selected by
   instr[3:2] alone:
     00 -> B-imm (BRANCH 1100011)
     11 -> J-imm (JAL 1101111)
     else -> U-imm (AUIPC 0010111)
   This replaces imm_gen's 7-bit opcode case (2-3 LUT levels) with one
   LUT4/MUX2 level per bit. For every other opcode pc_imm is a
   don't-care. JALR's target comes from the EX AGU.
   imm_gen stays as it is for ID/EX.imm and the LUI pre_result.

D. PC D-input ordering: pc_imm enters at the last mux level.
     pc_d = (pred && !redirect_q) ? pc_imm
            : (redirect_q ? target_q : pc + 4)
     CE   = redirect_q || !stall_if
   The pred select (opcode compare plus the flop-fed ctr) resolves in
   parallel with the carry chain.

Resulting fetch path: io_imemData flop -> 1 LUT imm select -> 32-bit
carry chain -> 1 LUT -> pc D, estimated at 6-7 ns. That is well under
the ~10.1 ns ALU loop, which stays the only limiter. The regfile-read
and decoder -> pre_result cones from r5s0 and r5s1 each also lose the
NOP-mux LUT.

RVFI is unchanged. pc_next, trap and reg_write keep the resolved
outcome computed exactly as today. Killed slots never retire.

Forecast:
  - Cycles: ~4.30M, as measured on r5s2. The cycle count does not
    depend on changes B-D.
  - Fmax: 105-108 MHz median. The predictor costs about +200 LUT (about
    1% from placement pressure), and removing the r5s0/r5s2 prefix
    gains about +1-2%.
  - Fitness: 10 x f / 4.30M = 244-251 iter/s, about +4-7%. The central
    estimate is +6%.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r6s2 (regression, -5.32%): Rebuilding r5s2's predictor with a shortened fetch path scored 222.81 vs r5s2's 241.82. The changes were a raw IF word with the imem-stall bubble moved into the narrow ID/EX flush, a separate instr[3:2]-selected B/J/U immediate in front of the shared pc+imm adder, and pc_imm moved to the last pc_d mux level. If cycles stayed at r5s2's ~4.30M as designed, this implies about 96 MHz vs 103.9, an ~8% Fmax loss where +1-2% was forecast. r6s0 made the same raw-IF-word/narrow-flush change on the same base and held ~108 MHz, so the loss most likely comes from the duplicate immediate decoder (a second load on every IF-word imm bit beside imm_gen, feeding an adder that also drives ID/EX.branch_target and the AUIPC pre_result) and the pc_d reordering. As with r6s1's queue head mux (also ~10% lost), extra logic hung on every IF-word bit costs more in route/fanout than the LUT level it saves, so the predictor should be kept exactly as r5s2 built it (shared imm_gen pc+imm, pred ? pc_imm : pc+4, redirect_q on top), and a reported worst path on this core should not be trimmed further unless a timing report on the new build confirms it is still the limiter.

title: Lane-local ID/EX operand copies (ALU / branch+AGU / DSP+DIV+store) with imm pre-muxed, load sign fill folded into the forward LUT
motivation:
Two rounds (r5s0, r6s0) removed 2-3 LUT levels from every reported cone
and both stopped at about 108 MHz, only +1.3% over r4s0's 106.5 MHz. The
r6s0 lesson says the limit is now route delay, not logic depth.
ID/EX.rs1_val has fanout 14 with a ~2.8 ns route, `sub` has fanout 33,
and the alu_src -> alu_b mux has fanout 71. The r4s0 report shows why:
one rs1_val/rs2_val flop pair drives the adder carry chain, the
shifter, the logic lane, SLT, the 32-bit branch-compare carry chain, the
AGU carry chain, the DSP (a fixed silicon site), the divider and the
store data. Placement has to stretch each operand flop between the DSP
column and the ALU/compare/AGU carry chains, so every EX cone (ALU ->
ex_result -> forward loop, compare -> PC, AGU -> BSRAM address) starts
with a long route. That route is shared by all the tied cones, which
is why cutting LUT levels inside any one of them did not move Fmax.
Only a few extra flops (FFs: 593 of ~15k) should shorten the start of
every cone at once, with no cycle cost.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Give each EX consumer group its own copy of the forwarded operand, so
each copy flop has low fanout and sits next to its consumer:
  1. ALU copy (a_alu, b_alu): feeds the adder, logic lane, shifter and
     SLT only. b_alu is pre-muxed in ID (alu_src ? imm : rs2), the way
     r5s0/r6s0 did it: imm enters at the EARLY forward level
     (rs2_early = alu_src ? imm : sel_mem ? .. : sel_wb ? .. : rf) and
     the ID side gates the late selects (sel2_ex/sel2_ld &= !alu_src,
     decoded from instr bits in parallel with the rd compares). No data
     level is added, and the fanout-71 alu_b mux leaves EX. Replicate
     `sub` per byte (4 flops) and the shamt bits b_alu[4:0] as a
     separate 5-bit copy for the shifter (sh_amt), so the adder's b
     input and the shifter's select tree do not share a net.
  2. Branch/AGU copy (a_cmp, b_cmp): a_cmp feeds the branch compare and
     the AGU (rs1 + imm); b_cmp is the raw rs2 for the compare.
  3. M/store copy (md_a, md_b): feeds the DSP multiplier (Gowin can pack
     these into the MULT36X36 input registers, which takes the DSP's
     fixed site out of the rs1_val placement entirely), the divider's
     start latch, and EX/MEM.write_data (store data). mul_a_sx/mul_b_sx
     stay as today (ID-built).
EX/MEM.rs1_val/rs2_val (RVFI only, pruned in the timed netlist) read
any copy (md_a/md_b), and RVFI stays unchanged.
All copies MUST carry `/* synthesis syn_preserve = 1 */` (and
syn_keep on the copy nets if needed), or GowinSynthesis merges the
equivalent registers back into one. Check the post-synthesis FF count
(~+190 FF expected) to confirm the copies survived.
Each copy is fed by its own last-level forward LUT (sel_ex ? ex_result :
sel_ld ? load_data : early) so that every forward LUT drives one flop.
ex_result and load_data then fan out to 3 LUTs per bit instead of 1,
which is a short local route, cheaper than one flop fanning out to 14
spread-out consumers.
Load-path companion cut (keeps r6s0's limiter, dmem BSRAM -> load
extract -> forward, from getting worse with the wider load_data
fanout). Fold the sign/zero fill of load_data[31:8] into the last-level
forward LUT. In ID, form sel?_ldw = sel?_ld & ld_hi_word/ld_b1_* and
sel?_ldf = sel?_ld & ld_sx_* (select-side only, from EX/MEM flops and
the ID compares). The forward LUT per upper bit is then
f(ex_result, early, rdata[j], ld_sign, sel_ex, sel_ldw, sel_ldf),
one LUT4+MUX2_LUT5/6 level, so the BSRAM path becomes
BSRAM -> ld_sign 4:1 -> forward -> flop (one LUT level less than now).
load_data (full extract) stays as is for MEM/WB.read_data.
Also take imem_ready off the instruction bits, as r6s0 did at no Fmax
cost. if_stage passes imem_data raw, valid = imem_ready, and the
imem-stall bubble joins flush_id (narrow: valid/ctrl/lane selects
only, gated by !dmem_stall and !ex_busy). Without this, cone (d)
(imem_ready -> NOP mux -> LUT-RAM address -> forward) stays at ~9.5 ns
and caps the result.
Cycle count is unchanged (4,527,646). Forecast: the operand route falls
from ~2.8 ns to ~1.0-1.3 ns on the ALU loop, the compare -> PC cone and
the AGU -> BSRAM cone together, minus ~0.2-0.3 ns of extra fanout on
ex_result/load_data. That gives about a 1.0-1.3 ns shorter period
(9.4 -> ~8.2-8.4 ns), a median Fmax of ~114-120 MHz, and fitness +6-12%.
The implementer should run `make timing` over all placement options,
compare the MEDIAN with r4s0's 106.5 MHz (not option 0 alone,
lesson r5s1), and check that the worst path's first route after the
ID/EX operand flop really got shorter. If syn_preserve is ignored and
the copies merge, try syn_maxfan on rs1_val/rs2_val or distinct
logically non-equivalent copies (e.g. md_b gated by a registered
is_mul|is_div|mem_write enable so it is not identical to b_cmp).

title: Lane-split operand delivery: replicated per-lane ID/EX operand and select flops (syn_preserve) on the r6s0 cut set
motivation:
Rounds 5 and 6 each cut every reported cone by 2-3 LUT levels, and both
stalled at about 108 MHz (r5s0 238.68, r6s0 238.28 vs the 235.32
champion at 106.5 MHz). LESSONS r6s0 concludes that logic depth no
longer predicts Fmax on this core. What limits it now is route delay on
a few high-fanout flops that every critical cone shares: ID/EX.rs1_val /
rs2_val (fanout about 14 per bit, with a ~2.8 ns route in the r6s0
report) and the one-hot select flops (`sub` has fanout 33). Each operand
bit fans out to the add/sub carry chain, the SLT/branch compare, the
barrel shifter (the heaviest consumer: one shifter input bit reaches
5-10 mux LUTs), the logic lane, the AGU adder that drives the dmem BSRAM
address, the DSP multiplier inputs and the divider. A flop with that
fanout cannot sit next to all of its loads, so every cone starts with
one long route. None of the round-4 to round-6 hypotheses changed this
operand-delivery structure; they only trimmed logic behind it.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure how operands reach EX. ID/EX gets one private operand
register per EX consumer group, each marked
`/* synthesis syn_preserve = 1 */` (plus `syn_keep` on the D net if
needed) so Gowin cannot merge the copies:
  A: rs1/rs2 for the add/sub + SLT + branch-compare lane (carry chains)
  B: rs1 (+ shamt = b[4:0]) for the shifter lane
  C: rs1/rs2 for the logic lane, AGU (rs1 + imm), store data,
     multiplier and divider
The same forward-mux output (rs1_fwd / rs2_fwd) drives all copies in
parallel. The copies sit at the end of the path, so they add no LUT
level and cost only one extra fanout on the forward LUT, which the
placer can put next to the copies. Each copy then drives about 3-5
loads, which the placer can place next to its lane. The high-fanout
one-hot selects get the same treatment: one copy of `sub` for the adder
and one for the compare/SLT, and one copy of sel_add/lop/sel_sr/sel_sll
for the result AND-OR. The EX lanes are rewired to read their private
copies. RVFI rs1_val/rs2_val read copy C, which is pruned in the bench
anyway.
Also carry over the cycle-neutral r6s0 cuts, because the operand-route
delay is shared by cones that are otherwise tied. Adding copies to only
one cone would let the others cap the clock, which is the r5s0/r6s0
failure mode. The cuts are:
  (1) Branch resolve in 2 LUTs into the PC mux (eq/lt from copy A
      straight into a pc_d select).
  (2) A one-LUT5 ex_result, with DIV moved behind the late-result
      interlock (late_result = mem_read | is_mul | is_div, divider
      result registered into EX/MEM like mul_p).
  (3) imem_ready kept off the instr / regfile-address bits: IF passes
      the raw imem word, and imem-stall bubbles are injected only
      through the narrow ID/EX valid+ctrl flush.
The total adds about 150-200 FFs (593 -> ~780, far below budget) and
almost no LUTs. Cycles do not change: every change is cycle-neutral
except the DIV-use bubble, which CoreMark almost never exercises. So
all of the gain has to come from Fmax. The target is about 115 MHz
median (from 106.5), i.e. roughly a 0.6-0.7 ns shorter operand route on
every tied cone.
Implementer check: run `make timing TARGET=bench` and compare the
MEDIAN over place options with 106.5 MHz, not option 0 alone. If Gowin
merged the copies (FF count barely rises), strengthen the attributes
(syn_preserve on each reg, or give the copies distinct reset/enable
structure) before evaluating.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r7s1 (regression, -12.63%): Unlike its sibling r7s0, this fed its syn_preserve lane-private ID/EX operand copies (A adder/compare, B shifter, C logic/AGU/MUL/DIV/store) and half-word select copies from one shared forward LUT per bit, which avoids the tripled ex_result/load_data loads that r7s0 blamed, and it carried over r6s0's cycle-neutral cuts, yet it scored 205.61, about 93 MHz vs r6s0's ~108 MHz at the designed ~4.53M cycles and even below r7s0's ~96 MHz; the most likely cause is that the ID/EX operand flop sits inside the single-cycle ALU -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop, so replicating it only moves the long route from flop -> spread-out lanes to forward LUT -> copies placed at those lanes on the same flop-to-flop path (this build also hung a second 32-bit compare subtractor and a 32-bit eq on copy A, so A still fed three wide structures), which means both forms of operand-flop duplication (per-copy or shared forward LUT) have now lost 10-13%, the next Fmax step must break or shorten the loop itself (an ALU-use bubble, or forwarding non-ALU consumers only from EX/MEM), and any future replication must first confirm from the post-synthesis FF count that the copies survived (none was reported for this run).

title: r5s2 decode predictor with a direct 1-cycle mispredict redirect (ID-registered flags) and a don't-care imm_gen head
motivation:
Measured history: r4s2's decode predictor used JAL plus BTFN-agree 128x2 LUT-RAM counters
with a direct EX redirect, which gave a 1-cycle mispredict penalty. It cut cycles by 294k
(4,491,817 -> 4,197,768). r5s2 ported the same predictor onto r4s0 with a REGISTERED
2-cycle redirect and cut only 232k (4,527,646 -> 4,295,423), at 103.9 MHz against r4s0's
106.5. Registering the redirect bought no Fmax: r5s0 and r6s0 both removed the
branch -> PC cone and stayed at ~108 MHz. It did cost about 62k cycles, one extra bubble
on each of the ~51k direction mispredicts and 13.8k JALRs.
r5s2's own worst path was the predictor fetch path:
  lfsr_1 (IF word bit 1, an opcode bit) -> u_id/u_imm -> pc+imm carry -> pred mux -> u_if/pc
with 15.146 ns arrival and 21 cells. That path, not the redirect, cost its ~2.5% Fmax.
The IPC ceiling of this category is ~359k bubbles (296k taken branches + 50k JAL + 14k
JALR, from the ISS). r4s2's structure already captures 82% of it, so the remaining lever
is to take back the 62k cycles lost to the registered redirect and the 2.5% Fmax lost to
the fetch path.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Start from r4s0 (the champion RTL in rtl/). Add r5s2's predictor EXACTLY as it was built:
a new branch_pred.sv, a 128x2 agree-with-BTFN LUT-RAM trained only from EX/MEM flops,
pred = valid && tgt_ok && (is_jal || is_br && (instr[31] ^ ctr[1])), and the SHARED
id_stage imm_gen -> pc+imm adder as the predicted target. Do not add a duplicate immediate
decoder or a second adder; r6s2 lost 8% doing that. The changes relative to r5s2 are:

1. Direct 1-cycle mispredict redirect, with no new LUT level on the r4s0 redirect cone.
   ID registers one-hot "redirect-when" flags into ID/EX, folding pred, funct3 and the
   target alignment together:
     f_eq  = redirect when rs1==rs2   (BEQ & !pred | BNE & pred)
     f_ne  = redirect when rs1!=rs2   (BNE & !pred | BEQ & pred)
     f_lt / f_ge / f_ltu / f_geu likewise for BLT/BGE/BLTU/BGEU
     f_jr  = is_jalr ; f_jal = is_jal & !pred
   A branch whose target has imm[1]=1 would trap when taken, so it may redirect only in the
   predicted-taken -> not-taken direction; its taken-direction flags are cleared in ID. pc
   is always 4-aligned, so misalign_branch is known in ID and leaves the EX redirect cone.
   EX then computes:
     redirect = f_eq&eq | f_ne&!eq | f_lt&lt | f_ge&!lt | f_ltu&ltu | f_geu&!ltu | f_jal | (f_jr & !misalign_jump)
   This is a 2-LUT resolve, at most as deep as r4s0's case-over-branch_op &
   is_branch. The target is precomputed in ID as
     alt_target = pred ? pc+4 : pc_imm
   and registered into ID/EX, so the EX target mux stays
     is_jalr ? {agu[31:1],0} : alt_target_q
   which has the same shape as r4s0. PC priority is redirect > (!stall: pred ? pc_imm : pc+4).
   flush_id = redirect || load_use, as in r4s0; a mispredict kills exactly 1 slot. RVFI and
   EX/MEM.pc_next / trap / reg_write semantics are unchanged; the resolved outcome is still
   computed from branch_taken as today.
2. Shorten the head of the reported worst path at zero area: imm_gen decodes from
   instr[6:2] with don't-cares. Every opcode that does not use an immediate (OP, FENCE,
   illegal encodings, instr[1:0]!=11) may produce any imm. Those instructions either have
   alu_src=0 or trap, and pred is gated by the decoder's exact is_br/is_jal. Group by the
   minimal opcode bits (I: LOAD/OP-IMM/JALR/SYSTEM, S, B, U, J) so each imm bit is ~1 LUT
   of opcode bits plus candidate instr bits instead of an exact 7-bit case followed by a
   mux. The value is still bit-exact for every legal immediate-using instruction, so
   formal/cosim are unaffected. This makes the shared adder input one level earlier on the
   path lfsr -> imm -> pc+imm -> pc (and on AUIPC/branch_target), and it removes logic
   rather than adding load on the IF word.
3. No RAS and no bigger table. JALRs (13.8k) stay at a 1-cycle redirect, and the remaining
   ~51k mispredicts are worth <1.2%, which does not justify the area that cost r3s2 13%.

Forecast. Cycles: r4s2's measured -294k with a 1-cycle penalty, rebased onto r4s0, gives
about 4.23-4.24M (-6.4%). Fmax: the redirect cone is no deeper than r4s0's, and the fetch
path loses one LUT at its head, so it should land between r5s2's 103.9 and r4s0's 106.5
median, at ~104.5-106. Fitness = 235.32 x 4.528/4.235 x (0.98..1.0) = 247-252,
i.e. +5..+7%. Area is about +200 LUT / +50 FF (r5s2: 2455 LUT, 652 FF).

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r7s2 (improvement, +7.09%): Rebuilding r5s2's decode predictor exactly (JAL + BTFN-agree 128x2 LUT-RAM, target from the shared imm_gen pc+imm adder) but with a direct 1-cycle mispredict redirect is the new champion at 252.01, just above its +5-7% forecast; if cycles reached the forecast ~4.23M, this implies about 106.7 MHz, level with r4s0's 106.5 MHz median, so the ~2% Fmax that r4s2 and r5s2 paid was not inherent to the predictor. title: Control-net fanout relief: side-effect-only ID/EX flush, load-use off the ID/EX data enables, reset-free data flops
motivation:
The champion r7s2 (252.01, 106.67 MHz median, 4.23M cycles) reports its worst
path as cpu/u_id/reg_q.rs2_val_0 -> 32-bit compare carry chain -> redirect ->
flush_id -> cpu/u_id/reg_q.ctrl.branch_op_2 (36 cells, slack -4.589 ns). The
endpoint is a bit that never needs clearing: a bubble's branch_op, alu_op,
mem_width, alu_src, lane selects etc. are never observed once valid,
reg_write, mem_read/mem_write, is_div, late_result and the f_* redirect flags
are 0. Today flush_id (= (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall) drives the
sync clear of the WHOLE ctrl_t struct plus 11 lane selects, 8 f_* flags,
late_result and valid (~45 flops), so the late EX compare -> redirect net has
a ~45+32 (PC) fanout. Likewise the IF-derived load_use hazard (imem BSRAM
word -> rd compare) sits in stall_id, which is the clock enable of ~200
ID/EX data flops, although the data fields of a load-use bubble are
don't-care. r6s0/r7s0/r7s1 showed that on this core route delay on

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion r7s2 (252.01, 106.67 MHz median, 4.23M cycles) reports its worst

mem_width, alu_src, lane selects etc. are never observed once valid,

sync clear of the WHOLE ctrl_t struct plus 11 lane selects, 8 f_* flags,

ID/EX data flops, although the data fields of a load-use bubble are
don't-care. r6s0/r7s0/r7s1 showed that on this core route delay on

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Three cycle-neutral control-path changes, all confined to id_stage.sv,
hazard_unit.sv, core.sv and the stage registers (no new IF-word loads, no
new logic in the ALU/forward loop, predictor untouched):

1. Side-effect-only ID/EX flush. On flush, clear ONLY valid,
   ctrl.reg_write, ctrl.mem_read, ctrl.mem_write, ctrl.is_div,
   ctrl.is_branch, ctrl.is_jump, late_result and the eight f_* flags
   (~16 flops). Every other ctrl_t field (alu_op, alu_src, branch_op,
   is_jalr, is_lui, is_auipc, mem_width, mem_sext, mem_to_reg, is_illegal)
   and the one-hot lane selects (sel_add, lop, sel_sll, sel_sr, sel_slt,
   sel_div, sel_pre, sel_mul_lo, sel_mul_hi) capture on the normal enable
   only. Safety argument (the implementer must check each consumer):
   ex_w_en = reg_write && ... -> no forward from a bubble; the divider req
   is ctrl.is_div -> no ex_busy; redirect is an OR of f_* terms (f_jr
   included) -> no redirect; EX/MEM.valid/reg_write/mem_* cleared -> no
   dmem access, no dmem_stall (ex_mem_mem_op), no regfile write, no RVFI
   retirement; branch_pred training is gated by EX/MEM valid && is_branch;
   sel_mul_lo/hi of a bubble only change EX/MEM.alu_or_mul of an entry
   whose reg_write is 0 (fwd_w_en = 0) and valid is 0. is_jump/is_branch
   are cleared so misalign_* cannot set anything on a bubble (belt and
   braces; they only affect is_illegal/reg_write). Keep late_result
   cleared so a bubble never raises a spurious load-use.

2. load_use off the ID/EX data enables. Split stall_id into
   stall_id_data = dmem_stall || ex_busy (both one LUT from flops: dmem
   ready flop & EX/MEM mem op, ID/EX is_div & div_done) for the data
   fields (pc, rs1_val, rs2_val, imm, rd, rs?_addr, instr, pre_result,
   branch_target, alt_target, mul_*_sx, sub, sh_arith, slt_u, ctr and the
   non-cleared ctrl/lane fields of change 1), and keep the full
   stall_id (with load_use) only where it gates the side-effect bits'
   capture (they are flushed anyway on load_use, so in practice the
   side-effect bits use: flush -> clear, else if !stall_id_data ->
   capture). On a load-use cycle the ID/EX data fields therefore capture
   the dependent instruction's (stale-operand) fields into a bubble whose
   valid/side-effect bits are 0; next cycle, with PC held (stall_if still
   includes load_use), the same IF word is decoded again with the load
   value now forwarded from EX/MEM and captured for real. PC hold, the
   hazard compare and flush stay exactly as today, so cycles are
   unchanged. Check: forward_unit uses ID/EX.rd with ex_w_en (= cleared
   reg_write), and hazard_unit uses ID/EX.late_result (cleared), so a
   bubble's rd is never matched.

3. Reset-free data flops. Drop the synchronous reset from pure data fields
   of the ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB registers (pc, operand values, imm,
   results, targets, instr, mem_* RVFI payload, load byte-lane selects,
   ctr), keeping reset only on valid and the side-effect/ctrl bits. This
   removes the reset|flush / reset-only SR merges on ~450 flops, cuts the
   number of distinct CE/SR control sets that constrain Gowin's LUT+FF
   slice packing, and shrinks the reset net fanout. The data fields of an
   entry with valid=0 are never observed (RVFI gates on valid;
   forwarding/regfile on reg_write). If riscv-formal or cosim complain
   about X-propagation on a specific field (e.g. MEM/WB.rd used by the
   forward compare, which is ANDed with wb_w_en), keep that one field
   reset; do not weaken any check.

exactly, which is a good implementation self-check). Fmax: the reported
compare -> redirect -> flush -> ctrl path loses ~30 of its ~45 endpoint
loads and the IF -> load_use net loses ~200 CE loads; with tied cones the
realistic outcome is a 2-6% Fmax gain (106.7 -> ~109-113 MHz median).
Compare the MEDIAN across placement options, not option 0.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r8s0 (regression, -0.68%): Relieving the two largest late-arriving control fanouts without changing cycles scored 250.30 vs 252.01, about 106.0 vs 106.7 MHz if cycles stayed at the designed 4.23M, which is well inside the place_option noise. The three changes were: flush_id now clears only the ~16 side-effect bits (valid, reg_write, mem_*, is_div, is_branch/is_jump, late_result, f_* flags) instead of the whole ctrl struct and lane selects; load_use is off the CE of ~200 ID/EX data flops (stall_id_data = dmem_stall || ex_busy, so a load-use bubble captures stale don't-care data); and the pipeline data fields no longer have a sync reset. The reported compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl endpoint was therefore only one of many near-tied paths, and cutting control-net fanout or merging CE/SR control sets buys no Fmax on this core, just as trimming LUT levels bought none in r5s0/r6s0. With r7s0/r7s1, this leaves the single-cycle ALU -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop as the likely ~106-108 MHz ceiling, and it must be broken (an ALU-use bubble, or EX/MEM-only forwarding for non-ALU consumers) rather than having load taken off its side nets.

title: Two-tier result network (EX-forward only add/logic/pre, shift/SLT/DIV late) + deferred wrong-path kill flop
motivation:
A fresh Gowin timing run of the r7s2 champion (place_option 0, 104.3 MHz)
shows about 25 paths within 0.15 ns, falling into two tied structural loops:
  (1) Path 1/3/4/22/25, data 9.554 ns: ID/EX.rs2_val -> cmp_lt/cmp_ltu
      carry chain -> 4-LUT redirect OR (redirect_Z_s1 fanout 33) ->
      flush_id (n2271, fanout 36) -> sync RESET of every ID/EX
      ctrl/sel/f_* flop. Paths 17/18 are the same net into u_if/pc CE.
  (2) Path 2/5/12-16/19/20, data 9.553 ns: ID/EX.ctrl.alu_src (fanout 74,
      2.4 ns route) -> alu_b mux -> 32-bit adder -> FOUR LUT levels of
      ex_result lane merge (sum | logic | sll | sr | slt | div | pre, the
      s9 -> s6 -> s3 -> s0 chain, ~1.9 ns of LUT) -> 1.43 ns route ->
      rs1_fwd LUT -> ID/EX.rs1_val. Paths 6/7/8/23/24 (rs1_val / imm ->
      ... -> rs?_val) are the same loop.
The load-forward cone (dmem DO -> ld_sign -> load_data -> rs1_fwd, 9.437)
sits ~0.1 ns behind. Earlier rounds cut one of these loops at a time
(r5s0, r6s0) and each time the other kept Fmax near 108 MHz. The operand
duplications (r7s0/r7s1) failed because they left the result merge in
the loop and multiplied its load. This hypothesis changes the structure of
both loops in the same build: fewer producer classes in the
single-cycle forward loop, and no combinational redirect into the ID/EX
register.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Two structural changes, both cycle-cheap:

A) Two-tier result network. Only the lanes that are ready early in EX
   stay in the single-cycle EX -> ID forward loop:
     ex_fast = ({32{sel_add}} & sum) | logic_out | ({32{sel_pre}} & pre_result)
   where pre_result is an ID/EX flop. Per bit this is sum, sel_add,
   a, b, lop[1:0], sel_pre, pre -> 2 LUT levels (LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5)
   instead of today's 4, and it removes the shifter/slt/div inputs from
   the merge tree. SLL/SRL/SRA, SLT/SLTU and DIV* join LOAD and MUL* in
   the "late_result" class. Their value is computed in EX as now and
   ORed into EX/MEM.alu_result (the ex_fast | late-lane OR sits only on
   the EX/MEM D input, off the forward loop). ID forwards them from
   EX/MEM via the existing mem_fwd_data path. An adjacent dependent takes
   the existing one-cycle late-use interlock
   (hazard_unit.id_ex_late_result: late_result = mem_read | mul | shift |
   slt | div, registered in ID). The forward_unit's ex select is gated
   by a registered ID/EX "ex_fwd_ok" (= reg_write & !late_result) so
   there is no new compare on the select side. The ISS estimate for
   CoreMark is ~1.5-2.5% more cycles: shifts and SLT(U) are ~7% of
   dynamic instructions, and roughly a third have a dependent directly
   behind (crcu8/crcu16 loops, core_bench_state). Some of those slots
   already overlap imem-stall bubbles.
   Also pre-mux the ALU b operand in ID: a single extra ID/EX register
   alu_b_q = alu_src ? imm : rs2_fwd (captured beside rs2_val, fed by
   the same forward LUT output, so ex_result/load_data gain no new load).
   It feeds ONLY the add/sub, logic and shift lanes. rs2_val keeps
   feeding compare, store data, DSP and divider. This takes the fanout-74
   alu_src flop and its 2.4 ns route off the head of loop (2).
   (Unlike r7s0/r7s1 there is one copy, not three, and it is fed from
   the shared forward LUT, not a per-copy one.)

B) Deferred wrong-path kill. The EX redirect drives only the PC mux and
   one flop:  kill_q <= dmem_stall ? kill_q : redirect_eff.
   flush_id becomes load_use && !dmem_stall only, so the redirect no
   longer fans out to the ~36 ID/EX ctrl/sel/f_* RESET pins. The single
   wrong-path instruction that ID captures on the redirect edge is
   squashed in EX one cycle later using kill_q alone (a flop, so it
   stays parallel to the compare chain and adds no level):
     - redirect_eff = OR(f_* & cmp) & !kill_q. Fold !kill_q into the
       first-level f_* & cmp LUTs as a direct flop input, parallel to the
       carry chain, so the chain -> PC path gains no level.
     - ex_w_en &= !kill_q; hazard late_result term &= !kill_q
     - divider req &= !kill_q; ex_busy &= !kill_q
     - EX/MEM captures valid = 0 and ctrl = 0 (no mem op, no reg_write,
       no trap) when kill_q. That is a flop-driven clear on the EX/MEM
       enable side.
   Cycle count is unchanged: the wrong-path slot is killed in EX
   instead of ID, and the PC still redirects on the same edge.
   RVFI/order are unaffected because a killed slot never reaches MEM/WB
   valid.

Expected: loop (2) loses about 2 LUT levels plus the 2.4 ns alu_src
route (the adder now starts from a plain alu_b_q flop), and loop (1)
loses the flush_id LUT and its fanout-36 route (~1.5 ns). The next
cone is load-forward at ~9.44 ns, then the compare -> redirect -> PC
path at ~9.0 ns. Median Fmax goes from ~106.7 to ~113-116 MHz (+6-9%),
minus ~2% cycles from the new late-use bubbles: net about +5%.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r8s1 (regression, -3.46%): This build made three cuts. SLL/SR/SLT/DIV left the single-cycle EX -> ID forward merge (ex_fast = add | logic | pre, 2 LUT levels) and were forwarded from EX/MEM behind the late-use interlock. alu_b was pre-muxed in ID, which took the fanout-74 alu_src flop off the adder head. The redirect no longer drove flush_id, because a kill_q flop squashed the wrong-path slot in EX. It was forecast at +5% (113-116 MHz for ~2% more cycles) but scored 243.30 vs 252.01, which is about 105 MHz vs 106.7 if cycles rose as designed, so it gained no Fmax and the new shift/SLT-use bubbles were pure loss. The forecast ignored its own timing report: the untouched load-forward cone (dmem BSRAM DO -> ld_sign -> load_data -> rs1_fwd -> ID/EX, 9.437 ns) sat only 0.12 ns (~1%) behind the two 9.55 ns loops it cut, so the best case was ~1%. An Fmax forecast must therefore be capped at the next-worst untouched cone in the report, and cycles (new interlocks, lanes forwarded late) should be traded for Fmax only when that cone is several percent behind. On this core load_data enters the same forward LUT as ex_result, so no EX-side shortening of the forward loop can beat the load path unless that path is cut in the same build.

title: Predictor-driven loop stream buffer: replay short predicted-taken backward loops from a 16x32 LUT-RAM so imem stalls are ignored inside them
motivation:
The direction/target predictor is nearly exhausted: r7s2 (champion, 252.01,
106.7 MHz, 4.23M cycles) leaves only ~51k direction mispredicts + ~13.8k
JALRs (<1.5% of cycles). The largest remaining cycle loss in the front end
is the imem backpressure: io_imemReady is a request-independent per-cycle
xorshift draw that is low 28/128 = 22% of cycles (fpga/bench_stall_gen.sv),
so every fetched instruction costs 1/0.78 = 1.28 cycles on average, i.e.
~0.28 stall cycles per instruction, only partly overlapped by load-use /
dmem / divide stalls. At ~2.7-2.9M retired instructions that is roughly
600-750k cycles (14-18% of the 4.23M). CoreMark's hot code is dominated by
short loops (core_list_find / list reverse, crcu8's 8-step bit loop,
matrix_mul/add/const inner loops), so a predictor-steered loop stream
buffer that supplies the instruction word from a small address-indexed
LUT-RAM while the predictor keeps fetch inside the loop hides the imem
stall for all those instructions. Unlike r5s1/r6s1's fetch queue, this
needs no push/pop enable on ~130 payload flops and no load_use-dependent
CE; the only thing on the IF word is one 2:1 mux that REPLACES the existing
NOP mux (r6s0 showed the raw-IF-word + narrow-flush shape holds ~108 MHz).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a loop stream buffer (LSB) driven by the existing decode-time
predictor (branch_pred.sv stays exactly as r7s2 built it).

Storage: buf[16] x 32-bit async-read LUT-RAM indexed by pc[5:2]
(syn_ramstyle distributed_ram, one sync write port), plus flops
start_q[31:2] (loop target), end_q[31:2] (loop branch pc), full_q, and a
2-bit mode {IDLE, CAPTURE, REPLAY}, and a registered hit_q.

Trigger (IF word, no new adder): a legal conditional BRANCH in the IF slot
that is predicted taken (pred) with a B-imm in [-60, -4], decoded from
IF-word bits only: imm[12]=instr[31]=1, imm[11]=instr[7]=1,
imm[10:6]=instr[30:26]=5'b11111 and imm[5:2]={instr[25],instr[11:9]}!=0
(imm[1]=instr[8]=0 is already required by pred's tgt_ok). This keeps the
loop span <= 16 words so pc[5:2] indexes each loop word uniquely
(-64 would alias start and end). On a trigger with pc != end_q: start_q <= pc_imm,
end_q <= pc, full_q <= 0, mode <= CAPTURE. On a trigger with pc == end_q
(flop-vs-flop compare, early) and full_q: mode <= REPLAY.

Fill (idempotent, address-indexed, path-independent): whenever
mode == CAPTURE and io_imemReady, buf[pc[5:2]] <= imem_data. Because the
buffer is address-indexed and code is static, any word fetched at pc is
the correct content of pc regardless of the path that led there. full_q
is set when the loop branch (pc == end_q) is fetched after a sequential
pass that started at start_q with no redirect and no other predicted-taken
branch (a redirect or any other predicted-taken branch in CAPTURE clears
the pass flag; the next trigger re-arms). FENCE.I clears full_q/mode.

Replay: hit_q is the registered "the word at the NEXT pc is in the buffer":
  hit_d = (mode_next == REPLAY) && !redirect &&
          (stall_if ? hit_q
                    : (pc == end_q) ? pred        // loop-back to start_q
                                    : !pred);     // sequential in body
(pc == end_q is a flop-vs-flop compare, pred is the existing IF-word
prediction; no new logic after pc_imm.) Leaving the loop (loop branch
predicted not-taken, any other predicted-taken branch, any EX redirect)
drops mode to IDLE-with-full (re-entry on the next trigger at pc==end_q
costs nothing, so a mispredicted body branch only loses the rest of that
pass).

IF word: out.instr = hit_q ? buf[pc[5:2]] : imem_data (raw, no NOP mux);
out.valid = hit_q || io_imemReady. imem_ready moves off the instr bits
(r6s0 shape): a not-ready, non-hit fetch is killed through the existing
narrow ID/EX flush (valid/ctrl/selects/f_* only) and holds the PC:
  imem_stall = !io_imemReady && !hit_q   (hit_q is a flop)
and stall_if / flush_if / flush_id use imem_stall. branch_pred's valid
input stays tied to out.valid. The PC still presents pc on io_imemAddr
during replay; the returned word is simply ignored.

Why it helps: every instruction fetched in REPLAY costs exactly one cycle
instead of 1.28 on average. If ~35-45% of dynamic instructions sit in
<=16-instruction straight-line loop bodies whose loop branch is predicted
taken, this removes ~200-270k of the ~600-750k imem stall cycles, i.e.
-5 to -6.5% cycles (4.23M -> ~3.97-4.02M). Area is ~+60-90 LUT (8
LUT-RAM cells, ~62 control flops, a 30-bit equality, the IF-word mux that
replaces the NOP mux); nothing is added to the critical rs2_val -> compare
-> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl path except that flush_id's
imem term becomes the flop-gated imem_stall.

Correctness: RVFI is unaffected (insn is whatever word was issued, pc and
pc_wdata are architectural); riscv-formal never checks imem consistency,
and cosim runs static code. The buffer only ever returns the word
previously fetched from the same address.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r8s2 (regression, +3.63%): The predictor-steered 16x32 LUT-RAM loop stream buffer cut CoreMark cycles by more than its -5 to -6.5% forecast (3.88M vs 4.23M, -8.3%), so imem backpressure hidden inside short predicted-taken backward loops is a bigger IPC lever than the <1.5% the predictor has left, but median Fmax fell from 106.7 to 101.3 MHz (-5%), so the net +3.6% missed the bar even though both siblings scored lower. The Fmax cost came from the IF word: the planned async buffer read in front of the IF-word mux put the LUT-RAM read at the head of the decode -> forward -> ID/EX cone (77 MHz at place_option 0), and reading the buffer one cycle early into a 32-bit word register recovered most of that, yet the flop-selected 2:1 mux on every IF-word bit, the imem-stall term folded into flush_id and ~+56 LUT / +36 FF still cost ~5%, while r6s0's raw IF word held ~108 MHz and the worst path stayed the old compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl cone, which points to route/placement pressure rather than a new cone. This is the third build, after r6s1's queue head mux and r6s2's duplicate immediate decoder, in which logic added on the IF-word bits cost 5-10% Fmax, so a fetch-side IPC idea should be forecast net of ~5% Fmax unless its substitute word avoids the IF-word -> decode path.

title: Timing-neutral loop stream buffer: keep the champion's NOP-mux/flush shape, fold the replay word into that one IF-word LUT
motivation:
Pure Fmax micro-trims can no longer clear the 4.6% bar. The r7s2 champion's
timing report (r8s1 motivation) shows three tied cones: the compare ->
redirect -> flush_id/pc cone and the alu_src -> adder -> merge ->
forward -> rs?_val loop, both at 9.55 ns, and the dmem BSRAM DO ->
ld_sign -> load_data -> forward cone at 9.437 ns. There is no cycle-free
way to cut the load cone, so any cycle-neutral trim is capped at about
1.2% (r8s1 lesson), and r5s0, r6s0, r8s0 and r8s1 all stalled at
106-108 MHz. Every other small IPC lever (posted stores, false load-use
on I-type rs2 fields, mul-use, the remaining 1.5% of mispredicts) is
1.5% or less.
The one measured large lever is imem backpressure. r8s2's
predictor-steered 16-entry loop stream buffer cut cycles from 4.23M to
3.88M (-8.3%) but lost 5% Fmax (106.7 -> 101.3 MHz) and scored +3.6%,
about 1% short of the bar. Its fitness is 10 x Fmax / 3.88M, so at the
same cycle count the bar is passed at >= 102.3 MHz. That is a 1% Fmax
repair of an existing measured mechanism, which this micro_opt targets.
The r8s2 lesson identifies three costs on top of the unchanged worst
cone:
(a) The flop-selected 2:1 mux replaced the NOP mux, so imem_ready left
    the IF word.
(b) The imem-stall term was folded into flush_id. flush_id is the
    endpoint net of the critical compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX
    ctrl cone (fanout ~36), so this added a late-OR input and more route
    load to the critical path itself.
(c) About +56 LUT / +36 FF of placement pressure, mostly the 30-bit
    pc == end_q compare and the capture/pass bookkeeping.
In the timed netlist io_imemData is a flop (the LFSR in
core_bench_si.sv) and io_imemReady is a flop (bench_stall_gen). So the
champion's IF word is one LUT (flush ? NOP : data) on two early flop
outputs. Folding a third and fourth flop input into that same LUT
(a LUT4 per bit) adds no logic level, and leaving flush_id exactly as
it is keeps the critical cone byte-identical.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild r8s2's loop stream buffer (LSB) with its replay policy
unchanged, so cycles should again be about 3.88M. The integration is
changed so the champion's IF-word, flush_id and redirect structure
stays exactly as in r7s2.

1. IF word stays a single LUT per bit on flops only. Today:
     instr = !imem_ready ? NOP : imem_data
   New:
     instr = hit_q ? word_q : (!imem_ready ? NOP : imem_data)
   hit_q, word_q, imem_ready and imem_data are all flops, so each bit
   is one LUT4 (bits 0, 1, 4 get the NOP pattern), which is the same
   depth as today's NOP mux. The shape also folds the same way: a
   4-input LUT on early flops into the decoder, regfile LUT-RAM address
   and load-use LUT4s.
   imem_stall_eff = !imem_ready && !hit_q is a two-flop AND. It
   replaces !imem_ready in exactly the places where !imem_ready is
   used today: flush_if (out.valid) and stall_if. flush_id stays
   (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall, with no imem term (unlike
   r8s2). stall_id and the redirect/pc mux priority do not change.
   The branch predictor keeps reading the (possibly replayed) IF word
   through out.instr/out.valid, as today.

2. The buffer read is one cycle early and flop-addressed, so no LUT-RAM
   read sits in front of the IF word. A 16x32 LUT-RAM
   (syn_ramstyle distributed_ram, one sync write port) is indexed by
   pc[5:2]. word_q <= buf[ridx] is registered on every cycle where the
   PC advances. ridx is formed only from flops:
     ridx = at_end_q ? start_q[5:2] : pc[5:2] + 1
   at_end_q is a registered "pc == end_q", computed one cycle ahead as
   next_pc == end_q, or incrementally as described below. When the PC
   holds (stall_if and no redirect), word_q and hit_q hold.
   pred/pc_imm do not feed ridx: in REPLAY the next PC is either
   sequential or the loop-back to start_q, and any other predicted-taken
   or redirect outcome drops hit_d (as in r8s2).

3. Less bookkeeping area, which addresses cost (c):
   - end_q stores the loop-branch PC. at_end_q is maintained as a
     down-counter: on the loop-back to start_q it loads
     (end_q - start_q) >> 2, and it decrements on each sequential
     advance, so at_end is cnt == 0. This is a 4-bit flop compare in
     place of r8s2's 30-bit pc == end_q equality on the fetch path.
     The trigger check "pc == end_q" (to re-arm REPLAY at the same
     loop) uses only the stored low bits end_q[5:2] plus a
     same-branch-seen flag that clears on any redirect, so no 30-bit
     comparator is needed. Where this is not provably safe, the
     implementer keeps the full compare but only in the CAPTURE/trigger
     path, which is never in the replay-hit path.
   - The trigger is r8s2's: a legal BRANCH in the IF slot, predicted
     taken, with B-imm in [-60, -4], decoded from IF-word bits that
     the branch predictor already loads. The capture pass flag and
     full_q are unchanged.
   - Target: at most +40 LUT / +45 FF over r7s2 (r8s2 used +99 LUT /
     +70 FF).

4. Correctness does not change from r8s2. The buffer only returns a
   word previously fetched from the same address. RVFI insn/pc/pc_wdata
   are architectural, and a replayed word is issued exactly like a
   fetched one, so formal (wrapper_si) and cosim are unaffected. A
   unit test checks the capture, replay, exit, redirect-during-replay
   and stall-during-replay sequences.

Forecast: cycles about 3.88M (r8s2 measured). If the median Fmax
recovers to 103.5-105.5 MHz (between r8s2's 101.3 and the champion's
106.7), fitness is 267-272, i.e. +6 to +8%. The break-even with the
4.6% bar is about 102.3 MHz. Before handing off, the implementer must
compare against the champion's MEDIAN across place options, not
option 0 (r5s1 lesson), and must check that the worst path is still
one of the three pre-existing cones and does not start at hit_q/word_q.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r9s0 (improvement, +7.88%): Rebuilding r8s2's loop stream buffer with the same replay policy but with the champion's IF-word and flush structure is the new champion at 271.88, at the top of its +6-8% forecast. The IF word stayed a single LUT4 per bit on four flops (instr = hit_q ? word_q : imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP, where io_imemData/io_imemReady are bench flops and word_q is read one cycle early from a pc[5:2]-indexed LUT-RAM). This shows that substitute-word logic on the IF word does not inherently cost the 5-10% Fmax seen in r6s1, r6s2 and r8s2: it is nearly free when it stays one LUT on early flops, the same depth as the NOP mux it replaces, and adds no input to the critical flush_id net. All three of r8s2's costs (the 2:1 mux replacing the NOP mux, the imem term on flush_id, and the extra area) were removed in the same build, so their individual shares cannot be separated, and it is unconfirmed whether the +40 LUT area target was met.

title: L0 instruction cache (64-word direct-mapped LUT-RAM) with the IF word always taken from a plain word flop
motivation:
The ~22% imem backpressure is the largest cycle sink left on this core. With
an undecoupled front end, about one cycle in five is a fetch bubble
(~0.8-0.9M of ~4.23M cycles). The predictor has <1.5% left, and the
ALU/forward/load loops keep Fmax at ~106-108 MHz (r5s0, r6s0, r8s0, r8s1).
r8s2's 16-entry loop stream buffer showed that hiding imem stalls is a large
IPC lever: cycles fell 8.3%, from 4.23M to 3.88M. It still lost ~5% Fmax. The
cause was a flop-selected 2:1 mux (buffer word vs imem_data) on every IF-word
bit in front of decode. r6s1's queue head mux and r6s2's duplicate immediate
decoder confirm that logic on the IF-word -> decode path costs 5-10% Fmax.
In the timed netlist io_imemData comes from an LFSR flop, so the champion's
decode cone starts from a bare flop. The substitute word has to keep that
property.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a small direct-mapped L0 instruction cache and make it the only source of
the IF word. No imem_data/buffer mux is in front of decode.
  * Storage: 64 x 32 instruction array plus a 64 x (tag + valid) array in
    distributed LUT-RAM (syn_ramstyle distributed_ram). The index is pc[7:2]
    and the tag is pc[19:8]. There is one sync write port, used only by the
    miss fill.
  * Read one cycle early: at every clock edge, word_q <= ins[pc_d[7:2]] and
    tag_q <= tag[pc_d[7:2]]. pc_d is the pc flop's existing D input
    (redirect ? target : stall ? pc : pred ? pc_imm : pc+4). Only the 6 index
    bits enter the LUT-RAM address. Those are the low bits of the pc+imm and
    redirect-target carry chains, so they arrive early. The IF word handed to
    ID is word_q, a plain flop like the LFSR it replaces, so the whole
    decode/regfile/forward/imm cone keeps its current shape.
  * Hit in the IF cycle: hit = tag_valid_q && tag_q == pc[19:8], a flop vs
    flop compare. It drives only what imem_ready drives today (the IF valid
    into the narrow ID/EX flush and stall_if). It never drives the instr bits.
  * Miss: the IF slot is a bubble and pc holds. The fetch goes to imem at pc
    (imem_addr = pc, as today). On the first cycle with imem_ready, imem_data
    is written into ins/tag at pc and also into word_q through a 2:1 mux on
    word_q's D input, i.e. on the fill side, not after the flop. The next
    cycle hits. Miss cost is the imem wait plus 1 cycle, paid only on cold
    and conflict misses.
  * Hits ignore io_imemReady entirely. The bus handshake is honored because
    imem_data is consumed only on a ready cycle (the fill). Cached words are
    architecturally identical to memory: CoreMark has no self-modifying code,
    and FENCE.I stays a NOP. A defensive option is to invalidate everything
    on FENCE.I retirement.
  * Reset clears the valid bits with a 64-cycle sweep or a valid-flop vector
    (r3s0's written-valid trick), so no reset reaches the LUT-RAM.
Expected cycles: CoreMark's timed inner loops (crcu8, list find/reverse,
matrix mul/add, state scan) are each well under 64 words. A 64-word
direct-mapped L0 covers them and more than the 16-word predicted-backward
loop buffer in r8s2, which cut 8.3%. Forecast -9 to -12% cycles, net of
~1-2k miss-fill cycles per iteration.
Expected Fmax: the IF word stays a flop and hit gates only the valid/flush
bits, so r8s2's IF-word mux cost goes away. The new cost is the LUT-RAM read
(2 levels: RAM16 plus a MUX2/LUT 4:1) after the low pc_d bits, ending at
word_q/tag_q. The low index bits leave the pc+imm and redirect carry chains
within 2-3 bits of their start. ~+150-200 LUT means some placement pressure
(r3s2, r8s2), so forecast -2 to -4% Fmax. Net about +5 to +9%.

changes.description: New module. 64x32 instruction LUT-RAM and 64x(12-bit tag + valid) LUT-RAM (distributed_ram), async read at the index of pc_d registered into word_q/tag_q/tv_q on every clock. One sync write port for the miss fill. Valid is kept as a 64-bit flop vector cleared on reset, or as a reset sweep. Outputs word_q, a hit computed from the tag_q/pc flops, and a fill enable (miss && imem_ready). On a fill cycle word_q captures imem_data through a D-side mux.

Expose pc_d (the PC's D input, the existing redirect > stall > pred mux) to the icache. The IF payload becomes instr = word_q (no NOP mux on the instr bits) and valid = hit. imem_addr stays = pc. On a miss the PC holds (stall), and on a redirect the icache read follows pc_d as usual.
Replace imem_ready with the icache fetch-valid (hit) in stall_if and in the IF-valid/flush term, so ID/EX's narrow flush takes the miss bubble. dmem, load-use and div handling are unchanged.
