lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r9s1 (regression, -19.25%): The 64-word direct-mapped L0 icache scored 203.49 vs the r7s2 base of 252.01, which implies about 79-86 MHz vs 106.7 if cycles landed between r8s2's 3.88M and the unchanged 4.23M (no cycle count was reported), a ~20-25% Fmax loss where -2 to -4% was forecast. Its IF word was always the word_q flop, and hit = tag_q == pc[19:8] gated only valid/stall_if/flush_id. The most likely cause is that its "read one cycle early" was indexed by the next PC: the build read the ins/tag arrays at every candidate next PC and applied the PC flop's redirect > stall > pred choice after the arrays. That put the late selects (EX compare -> redirect, IF word -> load_use -> stall_if, IF word -> pred) and the IF word -> imm_gen -> pc+imm -> LUT-RAM -> word_q loop in front of ~45 word_q/tag_q flops, multiplied the LUT-RAM read ports, and again folded the imem-stall term into flush_id as r8s2 did. The forecast's argument that the low index bits leave the carry chains early ignored that the mux selects arrive late. Sibling r9s0 held ~105.5 MHz because it formed its read index from flops only (ridx = at_end_q ? start_q : pc[5:2] + 1) and let any redirect or other taken prediction fall back to imem. An early-read fetch structure on this core must therefore take its array address from flops and treat a redirect or predicted target as a miss in that cycle, not index it into the array.

title: Predictor-steered loop buffer v2: replay word enters as the stall-slot NOP substitute (imem_ready ? imem_data : alt_q), flush_id and the IF-word shape untouched
motivation:
r8s2's predictor-steered 16x32 loop stream buffer is the largest remaining IPC lever on
this core. It cut CoreMark cycles from 4.23M to 3.88M (-8.3%, i.e. +9.0% iter/cycle),
far more than the <1.5% the direction/target predictor has left (~51k mispredicts + 13.8k
JALRs). It failed only on Fmax: its median fell from 106.7 to 101.3 MHz (seeds
95.97/101.3/101.3), so it scored +3.6% instead of about +9%. Clearing the 4.6% bar with
r8s2's measured cycles only needs a median of about 102.4 MHz (106.7 x 1.046 / 1.090).
That means recovering about 1 MHz of r8s2's 5.4 MHz loss is enough.

r8s2 changed two things on paths that already exist, and both are avoidable:
 (1) It converted the IF word to the raw/narrow-flush shape and folded the new
     imem_stall = !imem_ready && !hit_q term into flush_id. flush_id is the endpoint
     control of the champion's reported critical cone (rs2_val -> compare -> redirect ->
     flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl, 36 cells), and r8s2's worst path was that same cone, 0.8 ns
     longer. Adding two inputs to that late LUT is the most direct suspect.
 (2) It replaced the champion's NOP mux (imem_ready, imem_data[i]) with
     hit_q ? word_q[i] : imem_data[i]. The select is a different flop, and the
     imem_ready handling moved elsewhere.
In the timed wrapper (fpga/core_bench_si.sv), io_imemData is a flop LFSR and io_imemReady
comes straight from a bench_stall_gen flop, so every input of the IF-word mux is a flop.
A third flop input per bit (alt_q) therefore adds no late arrival; it only takes one LUT
input. The IF word is imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP, and an imem-stall slot is a valid=0
NOP that no flush logic sees.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild r8s2's loop buffer on the r7s2 champion, but have the buffer word REPLACE ONLY THE
NOP CONSTANT of the existing stall mux. Nothing else on the IF word, flush_id or the ID/EX
flush changes.

IF word (if_stage):
    out.instr = io_imemReady ? imem_data : alt_q        // was: imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP
    out.valid = io_imemReady || hit_q
alt_q is a 32-bit register that holds either the buffered word for the CURRENT pc (hit_q=1)
or the NOP 0x00000013 (hit_q=0). Per bit, the IF word stays a 2:1 mux selected by the
same early imem_ready net as today, and the only new input is one early flop. Both
sources are the same word when hit_q=1 (io_imemAddr = pc always), so the select can stay
imem_ready alone. This is the smallest possible change to the IF-word -> decode ->
forward -> ID/EX cone: no new select net, no raw-IF conversion, no NOP moved elsewhere.
flush_id stays exactly (load_use || redirect) && !dmem_stall. An imem-stall slot is
still a valid=0 NOP, and a hit slot is a real valid instruction.
hazard_unit: imem_stall = !imem_ready && !hit_q (a flop and an early input) enters only
stall_if (PC CE) and flush_if (now just the valid term). load_use/redirect are unchanged.

Loop buffer (new rtl/loop_buf.sv, r8s2's proven policy): 16x32 distributed LUT-RAM indexed
by pc[5:2], start_q/end_q/full_q, and a mode flag (IDLE/CAPTURE/REPLAY).
  - Trigger: a legal BRANCH in the IF slot that is predicted taken (pred) with a
    B-imm in [-60,-4], decoded from IF-word bits only. It arms CAPTURE with
    start_q <= pc_imm and end_q <= pc. A sequential pass from start_q to end_q with no
    redirect and no other predicted-taken branch sets full_q. At the next trigger with
    pc == end_q (flop-vs-flop compare) and full_q set, mode becomes REPLAY.
  - Capture: in CAPTURE, when imem_ready, buf[pc[5:2]] <= imem_data. The write is
    address-indexed and idempotent.
  - Next-word prefetch (keeps the LUT-RAM read off the IF word): the buffer is read
    asynchronously at the flop-derived next index nidx = (pc == end_q) ? start_q[5:2] :
    pc[5:2] + 1 and registered into alt_q. hit_d = replay && !redirect &&
    ((pc == end_q) ? pred : !pred). When hit_d is 0 (and on redirect/reset), alt_q loads
    the NOP. alt_q and hit_q hold on stall_if unless redirect, like the PC. So redirect
    and pred reach only the alt_q/hit_q D/SR inputs (flop endpoints), never the IF word.
  - Exit: loop branch predicted not-taken, any other predicted-taken branch, or any EX
    redirect -> leave REPLAY (full_q kept, so re-entry costs nothing). FENCE.I clears
    full_q.
branch_pred.sv, the decode predictor, the pc/next_pc mux and the redirect flags are
byte-identical to r7s2.

Why the gain should hold: cycles should match r8s2's measured 3.88M, because the policy is
the same. The buffer only returns words previously fetched from the same address, and
code is static. Fmax: the reported critical cone (compare -> redirect -> flush_id ->
ID/EX ctrl) has zero added inputs, unlike r8s2. The IF-word bits keep their select net
and gain one early flop input. Area is about +60-80 LUT and +70 FF (r8s2: +99 LUT,
+70 FF). Forecast: Fmax 103-106 MHz (between r8s2's 101.3 and the champion's 106.7)
x 3.88M cycles gives 265-273 iter/s, i.e. +5..+8%. It clears the bar if the median is
>= 102.4 MHz.

RVFI is unaffected: insn is the word issued, and pc/pc_wdata are architectural.
riscv-formal does not model imem consistency (the buffer only replays fetched words).
Cosim runs static code.

So a substitute-word register should be loaded unconditionally, with late control confined to a single valid flop, because a "flop endpoint" is not free when it adds 32+ loads to an already-critical net. Shrinking the IF-word mux below r9s0's one LUT4 per bit bought nothing.

title: Stall-held fetch word: reuse the loop buffer's word_q/hit_q to keep an imem word fetched while the PC is held
motivation:
The champion (r9s0, 271.88 at 105.5 MHz, 3.88M cycles) throws away every
instruction word that imem delivers while the PC is held for a non-fetch
reason (load-use / mul-use bubble, dmem stall, divider). The word is
dropped and the same address is fetched again on the release cycle, where
the bench stall generator refuses it ~22% of the time. Twelve rounds of
Fmax trimming have stalled at ~106-108 MHz (the ALU loop and the load
forward path are tied within ~1%), so this micro_opt slot spends zero
logic levels on the IF word and targets cycles only.

Measured before proposing (Verilator cosim, CoreMark --bench --istall
--dstall, scratch copies of cores/bench/rtl):
  - champion r9s0 RTL:                3,881,971 cycles (matches log.jsonl)
  - this change (stall-held word):    3,861,093 cycles (-0.54%), CRCs OK,
                                      "Correct operation validated."
  - rejected alternative, loop buffer widened 16 -> 32 words
    (pc[6:2], B-imm [-124,-4]):       3,899,684 cycles (+0.46%, WORSE:
    longer loops more often hold an internal predicted-taken branch and
    pay for capture passes that never replay), so the 16-word size is
    already the right one.
The gain is therefore small and measured; it is proposed as a
near-zero-area, zero-new-critical-load cycle cut to stack on the next
Fmax win, not as a standalone bar-clearer.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep a word fetched during a PC hold in the r9s0 loop buffer's existing
32-bit word_q register and 1-bit hit_q flop (hit_q already means "word_q
is the word at the current PC" and already hides imem stalls via
imem_stall = !imem_ready && !hit_q).

loop_buf.sv (the exact diff that was simulated):
  - word_q:
      if (!stall_if)   word_q <= mem[ridx];
      else if (!hit_q) word_q <= imem_data;
    The PC holds whenever stall_if && !redirect; on a redirect hit_q is
    cleared, so a word loaded then is a harmless don't-care. stall_if is
    already this register's CE; the D input becomes a 2:1 of the
    flop-indexed LUT-RAM read and the imem_data bench flop.
  - hit_q: a final arm on the control block, reached only when
    !redirect && stall_if:
      end else if (imem_ready) begin
        hit_q <= 1'b1;
      end
    cap_q, rep_q, cnt_q, at_end_q, full_q, start/dist/end are unchanged;
    on the next PC advance hit_q is recomputed exactly as today.
The IF word stays r9s0's single LUT4 per bit
(hit_q ? word_q : imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP); flush_id, the
redirect/PC mux, branch_pred and the hazard unit are byte-identical, and
no load is added to the redirect, pred or IF-word nets (the r9s2 lesson).

CAPTURE-mode invariant is preserved: the buffer write (cap_q && imem_ready
-> mem[pc[5:2]]) does not depend on stall_if, so a word held at an address
while cap_q = 1 was written into the buffer on the same cycle; cap_q is
raised only on a PC advance, which clears hit_q, so no held word can
predate the capture at that address. The held word is the word imem
returned for the current PC, so RVFI/cosim see the same instruction
stream (as with the existing replay).

Expected: cycles -0.5% (measured), Fmax neutral within place_option noise
(~+33 LUT for the word_q D mux). Net fitness about +0.5%, below the 4.6%
acceptance bar on its own.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r10s0 (regression, -2.30%): Keeping the word that imem delivers while the PC is held (word_q's D input becomes stall_if ? (hit_q ? word_q : imem_data) : mem[ridx], and hit_q is set on imem_ready) cut cycles by only the measured 0.54% (3.861M vs 3.882M), and at that cycle count 265.63 implies a median of about 102.6 MHz vs r9s0's 105.5 (-2.8%). The most likely cause is that the late stall_if net (IF word -> load_use, dmem stall, divider) went from being only word_q's CE to a LUT input on all 32 of its D inputs, which is the same "32 new loads on an already-late net" cost that r9s2 paid with redirect/pred on alt_q. The loss is also inside r9s0's own ~4% placement spread (101.2-105.5 MHz), so a sub-1% cycle-only change cannot be measured against Fmax noise and should not take a slot on its own; if it is stacked on another change, it must add no load to late nets such as stall_if. The pre-run sweep also showed that widening the loop buffer from 16 to 32 words raised cycles by 0.46%, because longer loops more often contain a predicted-taken inner branch and pay for capture passes that never replay, so 16 words remains the right size.

title: Loop buffer with per-slot next-index table: replay loops that contain internal taken branches (32-word window)
motivation:
After r9s0 the core runs ~3.88M cycles at ~105.5 MHz. Several rounds (r5s0, r6s0,
r7s0/r7s1, r8s0, r8s1) spent their effort on Fmax and all stalled at ~106-108 MHz,
because the ALU -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop and the dmem BSRAM ->
load_data -> forward path are tied at ~9.5 ns. Cycles are the lever that is still
moving. The bench drives imem_ready i.i.d. per cycle at 100/128, so every fetch
served from imem costs 0.28 expected stall cycles. r8s2/r9s0 showed this is the
biggest remaining cycle bucket: a 16-word loop stream buffer alone cut cycles 8.3%
(4.23M -> 3.88M). By the same estimate, about 0.4M imem stall cycles (~10%) are
still left. The r9s0 buffer drops to IDLE on any predicted-taken fetch inside the
loop body except the loop branch itself. It also only covers loops of 16 words or
fewer. Many hot CoreMark loops, such as crcu8's bit loop with its `if (x16)`,
list-find/compare loops and the matrix loops with conditional bodies, contain a
taken forward branch. They are fetched from imem on every iteration and pay the
full 22% backpressure.
r9s0/r9s1/r9s2 fixed the timing rules for such a structure:
  (1) The IF word stays one LUT4 per bit on flops:
      instr = hit_q ? word_q : imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP.
  (2) The array read address comes only from flops.
  (3) word_q is loaded unconditionally on !stall_if.
  (4) Late control (pred, redirect, stall_if) reaches only a 1-bit hit_q and a
      few narrow state flops. It never reaches the 32 word_q D inputs.
This proposal keeps all four rules.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Generalize loop_buf.sv from "sequential body plus one loop-back" to "any path inside
a 32-word window whose taken edges were recorded at capture time". Replace the
at_end_q/start_q special case with a per-slot next-index table.

Storage (distributed LUT-RAM, one sync write port, written only in CAPTURE):
  - mem[32] x 32: the instruction word at slot pc[6:2].
  - nxt[32] x 6: {tk, tgt_idx[4:0]}. tk = 1 means that at capture time this slot's
    word was predicted taken and its target lies inside the window. tgt_idx is
    that target's slot index (pc[6:2] + imm[6:2]). The last word of the loop body
    (the loop branch) gets tk = 1, tgt_idx = start slot, as at_end/start do today.
  - vld[32]: flop vector of slots captured since the trigger. Cleared on a trigger.

Early read (unchanged rule: index from flops only). Every !stall_if cycle does:
    ridx      = tk_q ? tgt_q : pc[6:2] + 1
    word_q   <= mem[ridx]                     (unconditional, CE = !stall_if)
    {tk_q, tgt_q} <= nxt[ridx]
    vld_q    <= vld[ridx]
tk_q/tgt_q always describe the slot at the current PC, so the "next word" index is
known one cycle ahead without looking at the IF word. This is what r9s0 does with
at_end_q/start_q, generalized to every slot.

Hit (1-bit flop, the only place late signals land):
    hit_q <= active && !redirect && vld_q && in_win_next && (pred == tk_q)
A disagreement between the predictor and the recorded edge (pred != tk_q) is just a
one-fetch miss: the next word comes from imem. The buffer stays active as long as
the PC stays inside the window. It drops to IDLE only on a redirect, on a
predicted-taken target outside the window, or on sequential flow past the window
end. Window membership is tracked with a 5-bit offset register off_q = pc - start
(words). It is updated on the PC-advance edge as off_q + 1, or as off_q + imm[6:2]
for a predicted-taken branch/JAL (4-bit/5-bit add on IF-word imm bits, feeding only
the 5 off_q flops and the 1-bit in-window check). This replaces r9s0's cnt_q/at_end_q.

Capture: the trigger is unchanged in spirit (legal BRANCH predicted taken, backward).
The B-imm range widens to [-124, -4], so the window is 32 words and pc[6:2] cannot
alias inside one loop. The trigger enters CAPTURE and clears vld. Every fetched word
(imem_ready while in the window) writes mem[pc[6:2]], sets vld, and writes
nxt[pc[6:2]] = {pred && target in window, pc[6:2] + imm[6:2]}. The pred/imm inputs
of the nxt write are only the D inputs of a 6-bit LUT-RAM write port and the write
enable, not IF-word or flush logic. When the loop branch is predicted taken again,
the mode changes to REPLAY. Slots not yet captured (vld = 0) simply miss and are
captured on that pass (CAPTURE and REPLAY merge into one "active" mode that writes
on every imem fetch). REARM on re-entry of the held loop is kept (full pc == end_q
compare on the trigger path only).

Correctness argument: hit_q = 1 only when word_q was read from the slot the PC
actually moved to. That slot is either pc+1 (when pred = 0 = tk_q) or the recorded
target (when pred = 1 = tk_q), and the recorded target index equals the target
that ID's pc + imm produces for the same word, because the word at that slot is
the same captured word. A slot's word is only ever a word previously fetched from
that same address in the current window, since the window base is fixed per
trigger and vld is cleared on a new trigger. Redirects clear hit_q and go to IDLE,
exactly as now. The pipeline, flush_id, the redirect/PC mux, hazard_unit
(imem_stall = !imem_ready && !hit_q) and if_stage's IF-word LUT stay
byte-identical to r9s0.

Expected effect. Cycles fall another 4-7%: roughly a third to a half of the
remaining ~0.4M imem stall cycles sit in loops of 32 words or fewer with internal
forward branches, or in loops of 17-32 words. Area rises by about 40-70 LUT
(32x32 + 32x6 LUT-RAM instead of 16x32, a 5-bit ridx mux, vld vector, off_q)
with no new logic on the IF word, the forward loop or flush_id. Fmax is expected
within the ~4% place_option noise (r9s0: 105.5 MHz). The forecast is net +5% at
medium-low confidence; the upside is ~+7% if the crc/list loops are fully covered.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r10s1 (regression, -7.53%): The 32-word loop buffer with a per-slot {tk, tgt} next-index table scored 251.42 vs r9s0's 271.88. No cycle count was reported, but a buffer that only turns imem misses into hits cannot plausibly add 7.5% cycles, so this implies about 97.6 MHz at r9s0's 3.88M cycles, or ~91-94 MHz if the forecast 4-7% cycle cut happened: a 7-14% Fmax loss where "within noise" was forecast. The read side kept r9s0's rules (flop-only ridx, unconditional word_q load, late control only on the 1-bit hit_q), so the most likely cause is that the write side and the window tracker broke them. mem was written from the IF word `instr` instead of the imem_data flop, which put 32 LUT-RAM write-data loads on the IF-word bits at the head of the decode -> forward cone. The LUT-RAM write enable and the nxt write data took pred and a 7-bit off_q + IF-word-imm add, and act_q/off_q/hit_q took the same pred -> add -> in-window chain. On top of that came ~2x the LUT-RAM and a 32-bit vld vector with a 32:1 read mux. So the timing rules for an early-read fetch structure also cover its write port and position state: capture should write imem_data under a flop-only enable, and anything derived from pred or IF-word immediates must stay off the array's write port and off multi-bit state.

title: Predictor-steered sequential replay buffer: grow the 16-word loop buffer into a 64-word tagged, flop-indexed replay store
motivation:
An ISS trace of the timed CoreMark region (2.92M instructions, -O3, 2K) run
through a model of r9s0's loop buffer and the 128x2 BTFN-agree predictor
reproduces the measured gain: 1.256M of 2.92M fetches hit the buffer, and
at ~0.28 exposed imem-stall cycles per fetch (22% geometric) that is ~0.35M
cycles, matching the 4.23M -> 3.88M drop. The same model shows the
predictor/loop-buffer policy is saturated. Direction mispredicts plus JALRs
are 58k (~1.5% of cycles). Letting the buffer keep loops with in-body
forward taken branches adds ~70 hits, and per-word valid bits or a 32-word
loop window add at most +52k hits (~0.4%). The 1.67M fetches that still
miss are not in short conditional-branch loops. They are the jump-threaded
core_state_transition (672k fetches, 0 hits, loops closed by JAL), the
fully unrolled crcu8 inside crc16/crcu32/crcu16 (400k, 0 hits) and the
non-loop parts of list/matrix, all code that re-executes but not as a
<=16-word backward branch. Remaining exposed imem stalls are ~0.47M cycles,
about 12% of the total.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Generalize loop_buf into a 64-word direct-mapped replay store that keeps
every structural rule that made r9s0 Fmax-neutral:
- Fill: every word fetched from imem (imem_ready && !hit_q) is written at
  pc[7:2] into a 64x32 data LUT-RAM and a 64x8 tag LUT-RAM (tag = pc[15:8]).
  A 64-bit valid vector (reset-cleared, also cleared by any FENCE/FENCE.I
  reaching EX) is set at pc[7:2]. Only pc[31:16] == 0 is cacheable (one
  flop-fed compare), so the tag stays 8 bits.
- Read one cycle early from flops only, never from a predicted or
  redirect target (r9s1's lesson): on every PC advance,
  ridx = at_end_q ? start_q : pc[7:2] + 1, and
  npc_q = at_end_q ? loop_start_pc : pc + 4.
  Register word_q <= data[ridx] unconditionally (r9s2's lesson) and
  hit_q <= valid[ridx] && tag[ridx] == npc_q[15:8] && npc_q[31:16] == 0,
  with late control applied only to the 1-bit hit_q: redirect, or a
  predicted-taken IF word that is not the tracked loop-back, forces
  hit_q = 0. The target of every taken transfer other than the loop
  branch's own back edge is therefore a miss that cycle, fetched from
  imem as today, and the words after it hit if they are resident.
- The LSB's loop tracking (trig/cnt/at_end_q/start_q) is kept so that the
  back edge of a short predicted-taken loop still hits via start_q. The
  separate 16x32 LSB array is removed.
- The IF word, flush_id, stall_if and the PC mux stay byte-identical to
  r9s0: instr = hit_q ? word_q : imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP (one LUT4 per
  bit on four flops), and imem_stall = !imem_ready && !hit_q.
The trace model (sequential-successor hits plus LSB loop-back hits,
direct-mapped 64 words) gives 1.954M hits vs 1.256M (+698k fetches, i.e.
about -195k cycles, -5.0%). 32 words would give +513k (-3.7%) and 128
words +1.0M (-7.3%) at twice the RAM and mux area. The new logic is
flop -> (pc+4 carry, LUT-RAM read, 8-bit compare, 64:1 valid mux) ->
hit_q/word_q. That is a flop-to-flop path well under 9.5 ns and off the
EX -> forward loop. Area is about +40 LUT-RAM units, a 4:1 read mux, 64
valid flops plus a 64:1 mux, and about +150-250 LUT, so it is forecast at
-1 to -2% Fmax. Net about +3-4%, low confidence.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r10s2 (regression, +0.11%): The 64-word direct-mapped replay store (64x32 data + 64x8 tag LUT-RAM filled from imem_data under a flop-only enable, ridx/npc formed from flops only, word_q loaded unconditionally, late redirect/pred control only on the 1-bit hit_q, IF word and flush_id byte-identical to r9s0) obeyed every timing rule learned in r9s0-r10s1, yet it only tied r9s0 (272.18 vs 271.88, well inside r9s0's ~4% placement spread) where +3-4% was forecast. No cycle count or Fmax was reported, but the ISS trace model that reproduced r9s0's 4.23M -> 3.88M drop forecast ~3.69M cycles (-5%), which would imply about 100.4 MHz vs 105.5 (-5%) rather than the forecast -1 to -2%. Unless the modelled hits did not materialize, the most likely cause is the added area itself: five times the storage bits of r9s0's 16x32 buffer (~+40 LUT-RAM units against r9s0's 48 in total), 64 valid flops behind a 64:1 read mux and an 8-bit tag compare, the same placement-pressure loss seen in r3s2 and r10s1. So the flop-only rules keep a fetch store off the critical cones but do not make its area free, and on this ~2.5k-LUT core, growing the store to chase the ~12% of cycles still lost to imem stalls appears to cost about as much Fmax as the cycles it hides. Any retry must report cycles and median Fmax separately, to tell a model miss from an Fmax loss, and should be forecast net of this ~5% Fmax cost unless the store stays close to r9s0's size.

title: Run-tracked loop buffer: always-write imem_data, replay on first loop-back (BRANCH or JAL), drop CAPTURE/end_q
motivation:
Champion r9s0 (271.88, ~105.5 MHz, 3.88M cycles) sits at the same
~106 MHz Fmax ceiling that r5s0, r6s0, r8s0 and r8s1 could not break
by trimming cones. Its worst path is the sub flop -> adder -> merge ->
forward -> rs2_val loop (30 cells, tied with the compare -> flush_id and
load -> forward cones), so a cycle-neutral Fmax trim is capped at ~1%.
The largest measured remaining lever is imem backpressure, about 0.47M
exposed stall cycles (~12%). r10s2's ISS model split this out. 672k
fetches in the jump-threaded core_state_transition get 0 buffer hits
because its per-state loops are closed by a backward JAL, which r9s0's
trigger ignores (it accepts only a backward BRANCH). Other loops lose a
whole capture pass on every entry of a loop the buffer does not already
hold. r10s0, r10s1 and r10s2 showed that growing the store or adding
load to late nets costs 3-7% Fmax. So the change must keep r9s0's
16x32 size, its flop-only read index, its unconditional word_q load and
its 1-LUT4 IF word, and should ideally cut area rather than add it.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace r9s0's CAPTURE mode and 30-bit REARM compare with a run
counter, and let a backward JAL trigger the buffer like a backward
BRANCH. The IF word, flush_id, the hazard/PC mux, ridx and word_q stay
byte-identical to r9s0.

1. Always-on write, flop-only enable. mem[pc[5:2]] <= imem_data
   whenever imem_ready (both are bench flops; today the enable is
   cap_q && imem_ready). Every write stores the true word at pc, so a
   slot is only ever overwritten by a correct word for an address with
   the same pc[5:2].
2. A 4-bit saturating run_q counts the consecutive sequential PC
   advances into the current pc: on redirect or a predicted-taken
   advance (pred && !stall_if) run_q <= 0, on a sequential advance
   (!stall_if) run_q <= sat15(run_q + 1), otherwise hold. Every
   advance consumed a word that is either written (imem_ready) or
   already correct (hit_q), so run_q >= dist means that slots
   start..end-1 hold the loop body, with start = end - 4*dist.
3. The trigger is widened to a JAL. dist = 16 - imm52, where imm52 =
   B-imm[5:2] {instr[25], instr[11:9]} for a BRANCH or J-imm[5:2]
   instr[25:22] for a JAL (bit 3 is instr[25] in both, so the mux is on
   3 bits). A backward JAL is decoded as instr[2] && instr[31] &&
   &instr[19:12] && instr[20] && &instr[30:26] && imm52 != 0 (pred
   already implies imm[1] = 0).
   On trig: load start_q/dist_q/cnt_q as today, and set
   run_ok = carry out of the 4-bit add run_q + imm52 (so dist <= run_q),
   then rep_q <= run_ok and cap_q <= !run_ok. hit_q <= 0, so the start
   word is fetched from imem exactly as r9s0's rearm does, and ridx stays
   flop-only. cap_q stays as r9s0's position-tracking pass. The
   always-on write fills the slots during that pass, so its loop_back
   still replays the start word from the buffer. REPLAY, loop_back
   (at_end_q && pred, which is also true for the JAL), cnt_q and the
   IDLE drop are unchanged.
4. Deleted: full_q, end_q[29:0], the 30-bit pc == end_q compare and
   the rearm branch, which run_ok subsumes because a re-entered loop
   arrives at its branch after a full sequential run. Net about -30 FF
   and -15 LUT.

Expected effect: loops that the buffer does not hold replay from their
second iteration instead of their third (r9s0 captures on pass 2 and
replays from pass 3). Short JAL-closed loops start to hit, mainly the
per-state loops in core_state_transition (~672k fetches at 0 hits
today). Rough estimate: +250-350k hits x 0.28 exposed stall cycles per
fetch, i.e. -2.5 to -4% cycles, at unchanged or slightly better Fmax,
because area goes down and no late net gains a load. run_q's only
inputs are redirect, pred and stall_if, and it feeds 4 flops through
one 4-bit add on the trig path, which r9s0 already has for start_q.
Before building, the implementer should run the CoreMark cosim cycle
count against r9s0's 3,881,971 cycles and report cycles and median
Fmax separately.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r11s0 (regression, +2.17%): This build kept r9s0's 16x32 store, flop-only ridx, unconditional word_q load and 1-LUT4 IF word, and changed three things: it writes imem_data on every imem_ready (a flop-only enable), it replaces CAPTURE's 30-bit end_q rearm compare with a 4-bit saturating sequential-run counter (so a loop replays from its 2nd iteration once run_q >= dist), and it lets a backward JAL trigger the buffer. It scored 277.77 vs r9s0's 271.88, the first r9s0 follow-up to beat it, but that is below the improvement bar and inside r9s0's ~4% placement spread. No cycle count was reported: if the forecast -2.5 to -4% cycles happened, the score implies about 103.5-105 MHz vs 105.5, and unchanged cycles would need an unlikely ~107.8 MHz, above the ~106-107 MHz ceiling. So the ~30 FF / ~15 LUT area cut most likely bought no Fmax, and the gain is the low end of the modelled extra hits. A fetch hit-policy change that cuts area is the only fetch-side lever that has netted positive, but at ~2% it is too small to clear the bar alone, so it should be stacked with an Fmax change, with cycles and median Fmax reported separately.

title: Hard-BSRAM L0 fetch store (1K-word, tagged, 2-ahead flop-indexed read into a fabric word register) merged into the loop buffer's word_q/hit_q
motivation:
About 12% of the r9s0 champion's 3.88M cycles are still lost to imem
backpressure (0.28 expected stall cycles per non-replayed fetch at 22%
stalls). Growing the fetch store is the one measured lever left: r10s2's
64-word tagged LUT-RAM replay store cut cycles to 3.69M (-5%) and obeyed
every flop-only timing rule, but it only tied, because ~+330 LUT and
80 LUT-RAM units of placement pressure cost ~5% Fmax (100.4 vs 105.5 MHz).
Fmax itself is pinned near 106 MHz by three tied cones (rs2_val ->
compare -> redirect, sub -> adder -> forward loop, dmem BSRAM DO -> load
forward) that r5s0-r8s1 could not move. So a fetch store is only worth it
if it adds almost no fabric. The Tang Nano 20K has ~46 18-Kbit BSRAM
blocks and the bench uses only ~4 (dmem): a hard-block store costs zero
LUT/LUT-RAM, holds 16x the words of r10s2's store, and its only fabric is
an index adder, a 9-bit tag compare and one 32-bit word register.
The catch is BSRAM clock-to-out (~3 ns, visible on the load cone), which
must never reach the IF word; hence the extra fabric register and a
read two fetches ahead.

80 LUT-RAM units of placement pressure cost ~5% Fmax (100.4 vs 105.5 MHz).
Fmax itself is pinned near 106 MHz by three tied cones (rs2_val ->
compare -> redirect, sub -> adder -> forward loop, dmem BSRAM DO -> load
forward) that r5s0-r8s1 could not move. So a fetch store is only worth it
if it adds almost no fabric. The Tang Nano 20K has ~46 18-Kbit BSRAM
blocks and the bench uses only ~4 (dmem): a hard-block store costs zero
LUT/LUT-RAM, holds 16x the words of r10s2's store, and its only fabric is
an index adder, a 9-bit tag compare and one 32-bit word register.
The catch is BSRAM clock-to-out (~3 ns, visible on the load cone), which
must never reach the IF word; hence the extra fabric register and a
read two fetches ahead.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/fetch_store.sv: a direct-mapped 1024-word instruction store in
inferred BSRAM (data 1024x32 + tag 1024x9 = {valid, pc[19:12]},
syn_ramstyle block_ram, initial contents all zero -> invalid), filled by
every successful fetch and read two fetches ahead with a flop-only
address, and merge its output into loop_buf's existing word_q/hit_q flops
so the IF word stays exactly r9s0's one LUT4 per bit
(hit_q ? word_q : imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP) and flush_id,
stall_id and the redirect/PC mux stay byte-identical.

1. Write port (flops only): when io_imemReady (a bench flop) is high,
   write mem[pc[11:2]] <= io_imemData and tag[pc[11:2]] <= {1, pc[19:12]}.
   No pred/redirect/IF-word term on the write address, data or enable
   (r10s1 lesson). Writing on a wrong-path/held PC is harmless: it is the
   true word at that address. Like the loop buffer, the store only ever
   returns a word previously fetched from the same address.

2. Read port, 2-ahead: invariant "during the cycle PC = p, the BSRAM read
   register holds index(p+4), and v1_q says it is on-path". The read
   address D input is pc[11:2] + 2 (pc flop + constant, carry chain from
   a flop only), with a matching rtag_q <= pc[19:12] of (pc + 8), both
   enabled by adv = !stall_if || redirect (the PC update enable, already
   computed). The BSRAM output is captured into a FABRIC register
   (keep it out of the BSRAM output register, e.g. syn_preserve /
   syn_keep, so the IF word never sees BSRAM tCO):
     store_word = DO_data, store_hit = v1_q && DO_valid && DO_tag == rtag_q
   computed from BSRAM DO + rtag_q flop (2 LUT levels) and consumed only
   as the D input of word_q/hit_q (below). v1_q <= 1 on a sequential
   advance, 0 on redirect or pred (the new PC is a miss for this cycle
   and the next: a redirect or predicted target is never indexed into the
   array, per the r9s1 lesson; target and target+4 fall back to imem).

3. Merge into loop_buf (one word_q, one hit_q): word_q's D becomes
     lsb_sel ? mem_lsb[ridx] : store_word,
     lsb_sel = rep_q || (cap_q && at_end_q)
   (flops only; the cap_q && at_end_q term keeps the CAPTURE -> REPLAY
   loop-back reading start_q from the LSB), loaded unconditionally on
   !stall_if exactly as today; hit_q's D keeps r9s0's late redirect/pred
   clearing on the 1-bit flop only, and ORs in store_hit when the loop
   buffer is not replaying (idle/capture) and the advance is sequential.
   Loop-back replay (the LSB's 1-ahead ridx = start_q) keeps covering
   short loops, which the 2-ahead store would miss twice per iteration;
   the store covers everything else that is fetched sequentially,
   i.e. straight-line code, long loop bodies, and every second+ word
   after a call/return/taken forward branch.
   imem_stall = !imem_ready && !hit_q, stall_if, out.valid unchanged.

Expected cycles: r10s2's 64-word store already reached 3.69M; with 16x
the capacity (CoreMark's hot kernels fit in 4 KB) but one extra miss
after each non-loop taken transfer, forecast 3.55-3.70M (-5 to -8.5%).
Fabric cost forecast +45-70 LUT / +50 FF, 0 LUT-RAM, +3 BSRAM, versus
r10s2's +330 LUT / +32 LUT-RAM units, so Fmax should stay within r9s0's
placement spread (101-105.5 MHz). Net +4 to +9%; the result must report
cycles and median Fmax separately so a model miss can be told from an
Fmax loss (r10s2 lesson). If a pre-eval `make timing` shows the BSRAM DO
-> tag compare -> hit_q/word_q path or the pc+8 index adder in the top
paths, register the tag compare one more stage rather than touching the
IF word.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r11s1 (improvement, +13.58%): Moving the fetch store out of fabric and into idle hard BSRAM is the new champion at 308.79 vs r9s0's 271.88, more than twice its +6% forecast. The store is a 1K-word direct-mapped data+tag array, written from imem_data under the flop-only imem_ready enable and read two fetches ahead at pc[11:2]+2 from the PC flop, with redirect/pred targets treated as misses. Its DO and tag compare feed only the D inputs of loop_buf's existing word_q/hit_q, so the IF word, flush_id and the PC mux stayed byte-identical to r9s0. No cycles or Fmax were reported, but with fitness ≈ 10 × MHz / Mcycles (which fits r7s2 and r9s0), the score needs about 3.42-3.47M cycles at r9s0's 105.5-107 MHz, below the forecast 3.55-3.70M. Reaching the forecast cycles instead would need 110-114 MHz, above the ~106-107 MHz ceiling set by the three tied cones. So Fmax most likely held, and the store hid nearly all of the ~12% of cycles lost to imem backpressure, which means the extra miss after each non-loop taken transfer cost less than modelled. This resolves r10s2's tie: the same idea in LUT-RAM (64 words, ~+330 LUT) lost ~5% Fmax to placement pressure, while in BSRAM, with a fabric capture register keeping BSRAM tCO off the IF word, 16x the capacity costs almost no fabric. On this Tang Nano 20K core (~4 of ~46 BSRAMs used), new storage should therefore go in unused hard blocks behind a flop-indexed early read and a fabric register, not in LUT-RAM. With imem stalls now largely hidden, the fetch-side IPC lever is close to exhausted, and the next gains must come from the ~106 MHz Fmax ceiling or from other stall sources (load-use, mispredict, DIV).

title: Lean predictor-steered replay store: keep r10s2's measured -5% cycles, cut its +329 LUT area and add JAL-closed loop back-edges
motivation:
The direction predictor has little left to give: direction mispredicts
plus JALRs are ~58k cycles, about 1.5% of the 3.88M. The one measured
lever still open in this category is predictor-steered fetch replay,
which hides the ~22% random imem backpressure. About 0.47M cycles
(~12%) are still exposed imem stalls.

r10s2 already showed where the cycles are. Its 64-entry direct-mapped,
flop-indexed replay store cut cycles from 3.88M to 3.69M (-5.0%,
measured, matching its ISS model). Its median Fmax was 100.4 MHz vs
r9s0's 105.5, so the net result was a tie (272.18 vs 271.88). That Fmax
loss is not a structural timing problem:
  - r10s2's placement-option-0 run reached 104.19 MHz, higher than
    r9s0's own option-0 run (101.18 MHz). Its reported worst path at
    option 0 (14.892 ns, pc -> bp -> lsb -> pc) was shorter than r9s0's
    (15.177 ns, the sub -> ALU -> forward -> rs2_val loop).
  - The loss shows up only in the other two placement options, which is
    the signature of placement/area pressure: +329 LUT4 (2554 -> 2883,
    +13%), +55 FF and +32 LUT-RAM cells.
At r9s0's median 105.5 MHz, r10s2's 3.69M cycles would score ~286
(+5.2%). So the task is to get r10s2's hit policy at a much smaller
logic footprint. The storage bits themselves (64x32 data) are what buy
the hits. The +329 LUT4 mostly came from the logic around them:
  - 64 reset-cleared valid flops behind a 64:1 read mux, plus the FENCE
    flash-clear.
  - A full r9s0 capture/replay FSM (cap/rep/full/end_q 30-bit compare
    and rearm) kept beside the store, although with a store that caches
    every fetched word the capture pass is redundant.
  - A wide tag (8 bits + a 16-bit upper-zero cacheability compare) done
    against a next-PC that was itself built with extra adders.
r10s2's ISS model also found that the jump-threaded
core_state_transition gets 0 hits (672k fetches, 23% of the timed
fetches). Its short state-stay loops are closed by a backward JAL, which
the r9s0 trigger ignores (it needs instr[2] = 0, i.e. a BRANCH). So
every back-edge target word in them misses.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace loop_buf with one lean replay store that keeps r10s2's measured
hit policy and every flop-only timing rule from r9s0-r10s2, and drop the
redundant logic.

1. Store: 64x32 data LUT-RAM plus a 64x8 tag LUT-RAM, direct-mapped at
   pc[7:2]. The tag word is {valid, pc[14:8]}. Code is cacheable iff
   pc[31:15] == 0, which is a registered flag computed from the PC flop
   one cycle ahead, like hit_q. Both RAMs are written from the
   io_imemData flop at pc[7:2] whenever imem_ready && cacheable_q. That
   write enable is flop-only: no pred, no IF-word bits, no stall_if on
   the write port (r10s1 lesson).
   The valid bit lives in the tag RAM with an `initial` 0 fill, so there
   are no 64 valid flops, no 64:1 valid mux and no flash clear. Reset
   does not clear it. That is safe because an entry only ever holds the
   word fetched from that same address, and imem is read-only (RV32IM
   here has no Zifencei; FENCE.I stays an architectural NOP as today).
2. Read one cycle early, from flops only (r9s0/r9s1 rule). ridx =
   at_end_q ? start_q : pc[7:2] + 1. word_q <= data[ridx] loads
   unconditionally on !stall_if. hit_q's D input is (tag[ridx] ==
   {1, npc_tag_q}) && npc_cacheable. It uses the flop-derived next-PC
   tag: loop start when at_end_q, otherwise pc + 4. Only the pc[14:8]
   slice and a carry-out are needed, from a registered pc + 4 upper-bit
   slice. The late controls (redirect, a predicted-taken IF word that
   is not the tracked back-edge) clear only the 1-bit hit_q, exactly as
   in r9s0.
3. Back-edge tracker: only start_q, a 4-bit cnt_q/dist_q and at_end_q
   remain. There is no cap/rep/full/end_q FSM, no 30-bit compare and no
   rearm path, because the store itself holds any word fetched before.
   The trigger now also accepts a backward JAL with imm in [-60, -4]
   (JAL: imm[5:2] = instr[25:22], upper bits instr[31], instr[30:26],
   instr[20], instr[19:12] all ones). A BRANCH keeps
   {instr[25], instr[11:9]}. imm52 is chosen by instr[2] (JAL = 1). This
   turns the core_state_transition stay-loops into back-edge hits.
4. The IF word stays r9s0's single LUT4 per bit (hit_q ? word_q :
   imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP). hazard_unit's imem_stall = !imem_ready
   && !hit_q is unchanged. flush_id, the PC register priority and
   pred ? pc_imm : pc + 4 stay byte-identical. branch_pred is unchanged.

Forecast: cycles ~3.62-3.69M. r10s2's measured 3.69M is the base, and
the JAL back-edges add up to ~2% more hits from core_state_transition.
Area target: at most +130 LUT4 and at most +25 FF over r9s0 (r10s2 was
+329 / +55). The LUT-RAM is the same +32 cells as r10s2. With that area,
median Fmax should land within ~2% of r9s0's 105.5 MHz, for a score of
about 278-291 (+2 to +7%). The implementer must report the cycle count,
the post-synthesis LUT4/FF/LUT-RAM counts and the per-seed Fmax
separately, so a model miss can be told apart from an area-driven Fmax
loss.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r11s2 (regression, +4.15%): A lean rebuild of r10s2's 64-entry LUT-RAM replay store scored 283.16, vs 272.18 for r10s2 and 271.88 for r9s0. Four things changed: the valid bit moved into the 64x8 tag LUT-RAM with an `initial` 0 fill and no reset or FENCE clear (safe because imem is read-only), replacing r10s2's 64 valid flops and 64:1 valid mux; the redundant capture/replay FSM and its 30-bit rearm compare were dropped; the 4-bit back-edge tracker was kept; and backward JALs were accepted as back-edges. No cycles or Fmax were reported, but at the forecast 3.62-3.69M cycles, fitness ≈ 10 × MHz / Mcycles implies about 102.5-104.5 MHz, vs about 100.4 for r10s2. So most of r10s2's ~5% Fmax loss most likely came from the flop and mux logic around the stored bits, not from the bits themselves. The design still sits about 1-3% below r9s0's 105.5 MHz and far below its BSRAM sibling r11s1 (308.79). If a fetch store has to live in fabric, its valid bits belong in the RAM itself rather than in flops, but on this core LUT-RAM fetch storage is a dead end next to idle BSRAM.

title: Fetch-store target-word pair: BSRAM entry keyed by the taken branch holds word(T) and word(T+4), read 2-ahead with the existing flop-only index, so a predicted-taken transfer no longer takes two imem fetches
motivation:
A fresh `make timing` on the champion (r11s1, 308.79 = 109.53 MHz median x
3.547M cycles) shows the top five paths tied within 0.02 ns (14.511-14.534
ns) on five different endpoints of the ALU -> ex_result -> forward ->
ID/EX loop (mul_a_sx, rs2_val_30, rs2_val_28, rs1_val_20, rs1_val_15), so
a single-endpoint Fmax micro-opt (e.g. moving the mul_a_sx AND to EX) is
capped at ~0% (r5s0/r6s0/r8s0/r8s1 lessons). The cheapest remaining lever
is cycles that fetch still loses: after every predicted-taken transfer
B -> T that the loop buffer does not replay, fetch_store has v1_q = 0, so
BOTH word(T) and word(T+4) come from imem at 22% stall (0.28 expected
stall cycles each, ~0.56 per transfer). The store already reads index
pc+8 two fetches ahead from the PC flop; during the cycle PC = B-4 that
read returns entry(B), so any payload stored with entry(B) arrives in a
flop one full cycle before B is even in IF, with no pred/IF-word term on
the BSRAM address (the r9s1 rule).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a second BSRAM array tgt[1024] = {valid, tag[7:0], word(T), word(T+4)}
(~2-3 more of the ~39 idle BSRAMs, 0 LUT-RAM) sharing fetch_store's read
address pc[11:2]+2 and read enable (!stall_if), i.e. read 2-ahead with a
flop-only index exactly like the data array.
1. Capture: its DO + tag compare (tag == pc[19:12], same form as
   store_hit) is registered into fabric flops tw0_q, tw1_q, tw_hit_q on
   the PC-advance edge (keeps BSRAM tCO off every late net). While PC = B,
   tw_hit_q says tw0_q/tw1_q are word(T)/word(T+4) of the transfer last
   taken from B.
2. Use (flop selects on the wide D, late control only on 1-bit flops):
   word_q D becomes tw_sel ? tw0_q : (lsb_sel ? mem[ridx] : store_word)
   with tw_sel = tw_hit_q && !lsb_sel (flops only; pred is NOT on the
   32 word_q D inputs, per r9s2). hit_q D ORs (pred && tw_hit_q &&
   !lsb_sel) and the sequential store_hit term is masked by !tw_hit_q
   (a B with a stored target never claims its own fall-through hit; the
   1-bit hit_q is the only place pred/redirect enter, as today). A
   phase flop ph_q <= (!stall_if) & pred & tw_hit_q & !lsb_sel then
   loads word_q <= tw1_q (flop select) on the next advance and sets
   hit_q if that advance is sequential, so T and T+4 are both hits;
   fetch_store's v1_q/2-ahead read resumes at T+8 unchanged.
3. Fill (flop-only write port): pred_q/idx_q (B's index + tag, registered
   from the PC flop when the IF word advanced predicted-taken), then
   word(T) latched from io_imemData when imem_ready at PC=T, and the
   entry written {1, tag(B), word(T), word(T+4)} when imem_ready at
   PC=T+4 with the sequence unbroken (no redirect in between). Words are
   always the true imem words at those addresses, and the tag holds B,
   so a stale entry (different target after B's predictor flips, or a
   JAL at an aliased index) can only supply the word previously fetched
   at T for this same B: if the branch goes elsewhere, pred is 0 and
   hit_q stays 0; JALR and EX redirects never use the entry.
IF word, flush_id, hazard_unit, PC mux and the branch predictor stay
byte-identical (r9s0/r11s1 rules). Expected: -2.5 to -4% cycles (T and
T+4 hidden on non-loop taken branches/JALs/calls), fabric +~80 FF /
+~60 LUT, no new term on the tied ALU-loop cones; net +2-4% unless the

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r12s0 (regression, -6.39%): The BSRAM target-pair store scored 289.07 vs r11s1's 308.79 where +2-4% was forecast. It added a second 1Kx73 array keyed by a predicted-taken branch B, read 2-ahead from the PC flop, that returns word(T) and word(T+4). No cycles or Fmax were reported, but fitness ≈ 10 × MHz / Mcycles implies about 102.5 MHz at r11s1's unchanged 3.547M cycles, or 98-100 MHz at the forecast 3.40-3.46M, vs 109.53. So unless cycles rose, most of the loss is Fmax. The build kept r11s1's timing rules: a flop-only index, pred only on the 1-bit hit_q/ph_q/tw_hit_q, and an unchanged IF word. The most likely cause is fabric area. r11s1 fed its BSRAM DO only into the existing word_q/hit_q D inputs, while this build staged the payload in ~136 new fabric flops (tw0_q, tw1_q, the f_w0 fill latch and the 36-bit p1_q/p2_q key pipeline) and widened word_q's D mux from 2:1 to 4:1, next to the five tied ALU -> forward -> ID/EX cones, which is the r10s2 placement cost again. A smaller cycle cost adds to it: tw_hit_q masks the fall-through store hit, so every pass through a once-taken branch that is not predicted taken gives up the B+4 hit r11s1 already provided. So BSRAM storage is cheap only while its payload stays inside the block behind the existing capture register: a new BSRAM fetch structure should reuse word_q/hit_q rather than add wide fabric staging, and a new hit source must never disable an existing one.

title: Hard-BSRAM L0 load shadow: hide dmem backpressure on loads with a 4K-word tagged copy of data memory read in parallel with dmem
motivation:
r11s1 (308.79 at 109.53 MHz, 3.547M cycles) hid nearly all imem
backpressure by putting a 1K-word fetch store in idle hard BSRAM: the
Tang Nano 20K has ~46 BSRAM blocks and the core uses 7. The matching
data-side stall is still fully exposed. io_dmemReady is a per-cycle
pseudo-random flop (78% accept, independent of requests), and every
LOAD/STORE in MEM freezes the whole pipeline until it sees ready, at
0.28 expected stall cycles per memory op. CoreMark at -O3 issues about
20-22% loads. At ~2.9M retired instructions that is ~0.6M loads and
~170k frozen cycles (~5% of 3.55M), and all of it sits in the timed
region. The CoreMark data working set (2K block, stack, .data/.bss in
RAM 0x20000-0x2FFFF, rodata in FLASH) fits easily in 16 KB, so after
the first touch nearly every load could be served by an on-chip copy.
Fmax is pinned at ~106-110 MHz by three tied cones (ALU -> forward loop,
dmem DO -> load extract -> forward, compare -> redirect -> flush_id),
so an IPC change that adds no logic level to those cones and uses hard
blocks rather than fabric is the lever r11s1 showed works.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/load_shadow.sv: a direct-mapped 4096-word copy of data memory in
otherwise idle BSRAM, read in parallel with the bench dmem and used for
a LOAD in MEM exactly when io_dmemReady = 0 and the copy hits. That LOAD
then completes that cycle instead of freezing the pipeline.

1. Arrays (inferred block_ram, zero-init). There are four byte-lane data
   arrays of 4096x8, so byte stores need no BSRAM byte-enable inference,
   and one tag array of 4096 x {valid, tag[3:0]} (tag = addr[17:14],
   index = addr[13:2]). A word is eligible when mem_addr[31:18] == 0.
   This covers FLASH 0-128K and RAM 0x20000-0x2FFFF and excludes MMIO.
   It is computed in MEM from the EX/MEM.mem_addr flop, in parallel with
   BSRAM tCO. About 10 of the ~39 free blocks are used, with almost no
   fabric.
2. The read port is registered like the bench dmem. The read address is
   agu_sum[13:2], i.e. the same D input that the bench dmem BSRAM
   absorbs through EX/MEM.mem_addr, and the read enable is the EX/MEM
   enable (!stall_ex_mem). So in MEM, DO holds the entry for
   EX/MEM.mem_addr, for loads and stores alike.
   hit = valid && tag == mem_addr[17:14] && elig && !conflict_q.
3. The write port uses only MEM-cycle flops, BSRAM DO and
   io_dmemRData, with no IF/ID or redirect terms (r10s1 rule):
     - a LOAD completing from the bus (dmem_ready, not misaligned)
       writes all four lanes with io_dmemRData and tag {1, tag};
     - a STORE completing (dmem_ready, not misaligned) writes its byte
       lanes (dmem_wen) with the replicated write data. Its tag entry
       becomes {1, tag} if it is a full SW or the word hit (merge into a
       valid word), and {0, x} otherwise, so a partial store to an
       unheld word never leaves a stale word marked valid;
     - a shadow-hit LOAD under !dmem_ready writes nothing.
   Because the copy is written by every completing store and holds only
   words fetched or stored at that address, a hit always equals the
   architectural memory word (imem/FLASH is read-only to the core).
4. Read/write collision guard. A write lands on the same clock edge that
   captures the next memory op's read address. So
   conflict_q <= ex_mem is a mem op && agu_sum[13:2] == ex_mem.mem_addr[13:2]
   is registered on the EX/MEM enable (low adder bits leave the carry
   chain early; the implementer may compare fewer index bits, which only
   adds false conflicts). A load right behind an access to the same word
   then just behaves as today.
5. Stall. In hazard_unit,
   dmem_stall = !dmem_ready && ex_mem_mem_op && !(ex_mem_mem_read && sh_hit).
   This is BSRAM DO + two LUT levels (4-bit tag eq + valid/elig/conflict
   AND), about the depth of the existing IF word -> load_use -> stall_if
   net. Stores still stall exactly as today.
6. Load data without deepening the existing load cone. Build a second,
   parallel byte-lane extract from the shadow DO using the same EX
   pre-decoded ld_* select flops. In id_stage, add it as one more
   last-level source: sel?_ld splits into sel?_ldd = sel?_ld && dmem_ready
   and sel?_lds = sel?_ld && !dmem_ready (both built on the select side
   from flops and the existing IF-word rd compare). So the bench DO ->
   extract -> forward path keeps its depth and only its final mux gains
   one data input. MEM/WB.read_data / mem_rdata take
   dmem_ready ? bus : shadow, which is off every forward path and feeds
   RVFI and the regfile write.
The IF word, flush_id, the PC mux, the ALU/EX lanes and the fetch store
stay byte-identical to r11s1. RVFI is unchanged: a shadow-hit load
retires with mem_rdata equal to the true word and the same
addr/rmask. Formal is unaffected (rd_wdata stays consistent with the
reported mem_rdata), and the cosim ISS sees identical values.

Forecast: ~0.6M loads x 0.28 x ~97% hit rate ~= 160-170k cycles, i.e.
3.547M -> ~3.38-3.40M (-4.5 to -5%). Fmax: a new late term on the
dmem_stall net (BSRAM tCO + 3 LUT + CE fanout) and one more input on
the last-level forward mux should cost 0-2%, so the net is +3 to +5%.
Cycles and median Fmax must be reported separately.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r12s1 (regression, -4.59%): The data-side twin of r11s1 scored 294.63 vs 308.79 where +3-5% was forecast. It added a 4K-word tagged BSRAM copy of dmem (~10 blocks), read at the combinational agu_sum on the EX/MEM enable, so that a LOAD that hits completes under !dmem_ready. No cycles or Fmax were reported, but fitness ≈ 10 × MHz / Mcycles implies about 100 MHz at the forecast 3.38-3.40M cycles (104.5 MHz if no cycles were saved) vs 109.53, so the loss is Fmax. The most likely cause is that, unlike r11s1, the shadow's BSRAM DO is used in the same cycle it arrives. BSRAM tCO plus the tag compare now feeds sh_hit -> dmem_stall, which hazard_unit fans out to stall_if, stall_id, stall_ex_mem, hold_mem_wb and flush_id (via its !dmem_stall gate), so flush_id was not "byte-identical" as claimed. The same net also drives the shadow's own read enable, a DO -> CE loop. On top of that, the shadow extract became a 4th data input on the last-level rs?_fwd mux of the tied ALU -> forward -> ID/EX loop. A fetch store can hide its hit behind a fabric register because the PC is known two fetches ahead, but a load address exists only in EX, so any structure that skips dmem stalls has to put a RAM read and a compare on the global stall/flush net in MEM. On this core that costs more Fmax than the ~5% of cycles lost to dmem backpressure, so the dmem-stall lever is closed unless the hit can be decided from flops before MEM.

title: BSRAM branch-target instruction cache (BTIC): supply T and T+4 after every predicted-taken transfer, replacing loop_buf
motivation:
The r11s1 champion runs at 3.547M cycles and 109.5 MHz. Its BSRAM fetch store covers
sequential fetches, but a predicted-taken transfer (pred) clears v1_q and
hit_q. That leaves the target word T and T+4 both fetched from imem at a
22% i.i.d. per-cycle stall rate, about 0.28 expected stall cycles each.
The only exception is short backward loops that loop_buf replays.
Every other predicted-taken transfer still exposes two imem fetches:
JAL calls, forward taken branches, back-edges of loops longer than 16
words, and the JAL-closed state loops in core_state_transition (23% of
timed fetches, which the loop buffer never covered). With roughly 13% of
~2.85M instructions being taken transfers and about half of them not
replayed by loop_buf, that is ~150-180k exposed transfers x 2 words x
0.28, or about 80-100k cycles (2.3-2.8%).
The direction predictor itself has almost nothing left (~51k
mispredicts + 13.8k JALR ~ 1.5%), so the useful predictor lever is
steering fetch *storage* with the prediction. It must use the flop-only
rules from r9s0-r11s1 and idle hard BSRAM (r11s1: BSRAM storage costs
~no fabric; r10s2/r11s2: LUT-RAM storage costs ~5% Fmax).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a PowerPC-750-style branch-target instruction cache in idle BSRAM,
indexed exactly like the fetch store so its read is flop-only and two
fetches ahead. Delete loop_buf, which the BTIC plus the fetch store make
redundant, so the net fabric area stays roughly flat.

1. Storage: two BSRAM arrays, bt0 and bt1, each 512 x {valid, tag p[19:11],
   word[31:0]}. They are indexed by (p+4)[10:2], where p is the PC of the
   predicted-taken JAL/BRANCH. bt0 holds the word at the target T and
   bt1 the word at T+4. Use syn_ramstyle block_ram and an `initial` zero
   fill (all entries invalid). This takes about 4 blocks (512x36 x2 per
   array); 1024 entries with the fetch store's pc[19:12] tag are also
   fine (6 blocks). Either way the design stays well under 46.
   The (index of p+4, tag of p) pair identifies p exactly, the same
   convention the fetch store uses.
2. Read (flop-only): same address and enable as fetch_store: the index
   pc[11:2]+2 (or [10:2]) is registered on !stall_if. So while PC = p and
   v1_q = 1, DO0/DO1 hold the entry for branch p. The following are
   computed only from BSRAM DO and flops:
     bt_hit0 = v1_q && DO0.v && DO0.tag == pc tag
     w1ok_d  = v1_q && DO1.v && DO1.tag == pc tag
3. Word source on each PC advance (all selects are flops or raw BSRAM
   bits, with no pred, redirect or IF-word term on the 32 D inputs; see
   the r9s2 and r10s0 lessons):
     word_q <= tgt1_q ? w1_q : DO0.v ? DO0.word : store_word
     w1_q   <= DO1.word        (unconditional load on !stall_if)
     w1ok_q <= w1ok_d
   Late control touches only 1-bit flops:
     hit_q  <= redirect ? 0 : pred ? bt_hit0
               : tgt1_q ? w1ok_q : (!DO0.v && store_hit)
     tgt1_q <= !redirect && adv && pred && bt_hit0
   The IF word stays r9s0's single LUT4 per bit
   (hit_q ? word_q : imem_ready ? imem_data : NOP). flush_id, stall_id,
   hazard_unit and the redirect/PC mux stay byte-identical. When a stale
   BTIC entry exists but the branch is predicted not-taken, hit_q is 0
   and p+4 comes from imem, as it does today after a transfer. This case
   is rare and costs only speed, never correctness.
4. Fill (flop-only write ports, written from io_imemData under
   imem_ready; r10s1 lesson):
     on adv && pred && !redirect: wptr_q <= index(p+4), wtag_q <= p tag,
                                  st1_q <= 1  (PC becomes T)
     st1_q && imem_ready:         bt0[wptr_q] <= {1, wtag_q, imem_data}
     on adv from T: st2_q <= st1_q && !pred && !redirect (PC = T+4)
     st2_q && imem_ready:         bt1[wptr_q] <= {1, wtag_q, imem_data}
   st1_q and st2_q clear on any other advance or on redirect. The words
   are always the true words at T and T+4, because imem_addr = pc and
   code is read-only. Rewriting a word on a BTIC hit is harmless.
5. Coverage: after a BTIC-hit transfer, PC = T is served from w0 and
   T+4 from w1. The fetch store is valid again from T+8 (v1_q sets on
   the T -> T+4 advance). A branch at T+4 or later sees a valid BTIC
   lookup, so short loops are fully covered without loop_buf's
   capture/replay FSM, 16x32 LUT-RAM, 30-bit end_q compare or the
   LUT-RAM -> word_q mux. Removing loop_buf roughly offsets the ~80 new
   FFs (w1_q, flags, pointers) and the 2 tag compares.

Expected result: CoreMark cycles fall about 2.5-4% (3.547M -> ~3.42M),
because every correctly predicted taken transfer stops exposing two imem
fetches. Fmax should hold at r11s1's level, since new logic touches no
tied ALU/forward/load cone and fabric area is about flat. Report cycles
and median Fmax separately.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r12s2 (regression, -4.11%): The BTIC retry of r12s0's target-pair idea scored 296.11 vs r11s1's 308.79 where +3% was forecast. It used two BSRAM arrays sharing the fetch store's flop-only rd_idx to supply word(T) and word(T+4) after a predicted-taken transfer, and deleted loop_buf to keep fabric area flat. With ~80 new flops instead of r12s0's ~136 and a 3:1 instead of 4:1 word_q D mux, it recovered only ~2.4% over r12s0's 289.07. No cycles or Fmax were reported, but fitness ≈ 10 × MHz / Mcycles implies ~105 MHz at r11s1's 3.547M cycles, ~101 MHz at the forecast 3.42M, or +4.3% cycles (~3.70M) if 109.53 MHz held. Two constructs in the spec plausibly share the blame. First, word_q's source select is the raw, untagged BSRAM valid bit DO0.v, which puts BSRAM tCO on a 32-wide select net ahead of the capture register, where r11s1 only passed DO data bits straight through one LUT. Second, `hit_q <= !DO0.v && store_hit` lets any valid BTIC entry at index(pc+4), whatever its tag, veto the fetch-store hit. That costs every not-predicted-taken pass through a once-taken branch plus every aliasing sequential PC, which is r12s0's "new hit source disables an old one" flaw at wider scope. After two BSRAM target stores (r12s0, r12s2) lost 4-6% chasing a ~2.5% cycle prize that r11s1's own result suggested was over-modelled, the post-taken-transfer T/T+4 fetch lever should be treated as closed on this core. Any retry must keep raw BSRAM DO bits off both the word_q select and the hit veto, and must report cycles and median Fmax separately.

title: Load->branch interlock removal: branches fed by a LOAD/MUL in EX resolve one stage later in MEM from the MEM/WB flop
motivation:
Measured before proposing. `make timing TARGET=bench` on the r11s1
champion (place_option 0: 108.2 MHz, 2600 LUT / 702 FF / 7 BSRAM) shows
the top five paths tied within 0.023 ns (14.511-14.534 ns), all on the
ALU/shift -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop that r5s0-r8s1 could not
move, so an Fmax trim cannot clear the bar. A Python-ISS trace of the
-O3 CoreMark ELF (reference.py, first 4.5M instructions) counts the
late-result (load/mul-use) interlock bubbles by consumer:
  loads 547k, stores 142k; true load-use 204.8k, of which
  LOAD -> dependent BRANCH = 135.8k (66%, core_state lbu -> beq/bne,
  list/cmp loops); mul-use 35.7k; store-data-only deps 3.9k; false
  matches on unused rs1/rs2 fields only ~80.
So the one sizeable interlock lever is load -> branch, ~136k bubbles,
about 3.5-3.8% of the champion's ~3.55M cycles. A branch does not need
its operand in EX if it is allowed to resolve one stage later: when the
branch is in MEM, the LOAD is in WB and its value is the MEM/WB
read_data flop, so the late compare starts from flops, not from BSRAM DO.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Let a conditional BRANCH whose rs1 and/or rs2 is produced by the
late-result instruction (LOAD or MUL*) currently in ID/EX enter EX with
no bubble, and resolve it in MEM:
(1) hazard_unit: load_use no longer fires when the IF word is a BRANCH
    (opcode 1100011); instead id_stage registers lb_q (late branch) and
    lb1_q/lb2_q (which operand is late) into ID/EX. These are the same
    rd == rs compares, now only flop D inputs; the load_use net gets one
    opcode term folded into its existing compare LUTs.
(2) A late branch clears its ID-built f_* redirect flags (select-side,
    early), so EX never redirects for it; it carries f-flags, alt_target,
    lb1/lb2 and its forwarded (non-late) operands into EX/MEM.
(3) mem_stage: a = lb1 ? wb_w_data : rs1_val, b = lb2 ? wb_w_data :
    rs2_val (wb_w_data = MEM/WB mux of two flops), a second
    eq/lt/ltu compare, redirect_mem = lb_q && valid && (flag & cond ORed,
    same one-hot form as EX). If the producer did not write (misaligned
    load trapped, MEM/WB reg_write = 0), redirect_mem replays the branch
    itself (target = its pc, branch not retired: MEM/WB.valid = 0), so
    the rare trap case stays exact with no extra datapath.
(4) Redirect priority: redirect_mem (older) > EX redirect > pred.
    redirect_mem kills the EX slot (EX/MEM captures a bubble: valid and
    side-effect ctrl cleared) and flushes ID/EX; loop_buf / fetch_store /
    if_stage see redirect_any = redirect_mem | redirect. EX/MEM never
    holds while a branch sits in it (dmem_stall needs a mem op there), so
    the MEM resolve always advances.
(5) Predictor training moves from EX/MEM to MEM/WB flops (branch_taken /
    ctr / pc carried one stage further) so late branches train with
    their MEM-resolved outcome; RVFI pc_next for a late branch is
    computed in MEM.
Cycles: a correctly predicted late branch saves the 1-cycle bubble; a
mispredicted one costs 2 killed slots, the same as today's bubble + 1
flush, so the change never adds cycles. Forecast -3.3 to -3.8% cycles
(~117-135k of the 136k bubbles; the rest are mispredicted).
Fmax risk: the new MEM compare starts from MEM/WB flops (flop -> 1 LUT
-> 32-bit compare -> cond), about as deep as the EX compare, but it adds
one input to the redirect / flush_id / PC-mux nets that sit on the tied
compare -> redirect cone, and ~+120 LUT / ~+10 FF. Budget -1 to -2%
median Fmax; net +1.5 to +3%. Low confidence of clearing 4.6%.
Implementer: report cosim cycles and median Fmax separately.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-001-r13s0 (regression, -12.61%): Removing the load/MUL -> branch interlock (~136k bubbles, ~3.8% of cycles by ISS count) by resolving such branches in MEM scored 269.85 vs r11s1's 308.79, where +3% was forecast. The build added a second eq/lt/ltu compare on the MEM/WB wb_w_data mux. Its redirect_mem took top PC-mux priority and also drove flush_id, a new EX/MEM kill, loop_buf/fetch_store and MEM/WB.valid. The build also added an IF-word BRANCH-opcode term on load_use and IF-word rd == rs compares that clear the ID/EX f_* flags. No cycles or Fmax were reported, but fitness ≈ 10 × MHz / Mcycles implies about 92-96 MHz vs 109.53, a 13-16% loss against a 1-2% budget, whether cycles fell by the forecast ~3.5% or not at all. The most likely cause is that the same-cycle redirect_mem put a new 32-bit compare in front of every consumer of the already-tied compare -> redirect -> flush_id/PC cone, and the IF-word terms on the late load_use net may have added to it; both changed in the same build, so their shares cannot be separated. An interlock worth under 4% of cycles cannot pay for a new same-cycle redirect source on this core. Any retry should register the MEM resolve (a redirect_mem_q flop acting one cycle later, which costs one extra slot only on the few late branches that mispredict) so that the new compare feeds only flops, and it must report cycles and median Fmax separately.

title: Late branch resolve in MEM for load-dependent branches: remove the load-use bubble of ~135k load->branch pairs from the registered load value
motivation:
Measured with the Python ISS (test/cosim/reference.py) on the exact
CoreMark build (-O3, 2K, timed region between the MMIO markers):
2,922,016 retired instructions, 544,852 loads, 139,631 stores and
203,959 true load-use pairs (the hazard unit's raw-field check fires
204,039 times). So on the 3,547,028-cycle champion the load-use bubble
costs 5.75% of all cycles. By consumer: 135,320 are BRANCHES (list
find/compare loops, state machine, `lw; beqz`), 59,270 use the loaded
value as an ADDRESS (pointer chasing), and only 5,760 simple ALU ops,
3,189 shifts and 420 store-data. Fetch stalls are nearly all hidden
(r11s1), the predictor has <1.5% left, and five rounds of Fmax cuts
have stalled at ~106-110 MHz on tied cones, so load -> branch
(3.8% of cycles) is the largest single remaining cycle lever that does
not touch those cones.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Resolve a conditional branch whose operand is produced by the LOAD
directly ahead of it one stage later, in MEM, instead of bubbling it.

Key observation: a late-resolved branch that is predicted correctly
costs 0 cycles instead of today's 1 (the bubble); one that mispredicts
redirects from MEM and kills 3 younger slots (IF, ID, EX), exactly the
1 bubble + 2-slot EX redirect it pays today. So the IPC gain is the
full ~135k cycles (-3.8%) with no new penalty for mispredicts.

Hazard: load_use_hazard is not raised when ID/EX holds a LOAD
(ctrl.mem_read, not MUL) and the IF word is a legal BRANCH (the same
opcode/funct3 decode branch_pred already does on the IF word). ID marks
the branch late (late_a / late_b per operand matching ID/EX.rd), keeps
the forwarded value of the other operand, captures rs?_early (the
pre-load value, not ex_result) for the late operand as a trapped-load
fallback, and zeroes its f_* redirect-when flags in ID/EX so EX never
redirects on it. The f_* flags and alt_target ride into EX/MEM as
lf_* late flags.

MEM: in the late branch's MEM cycle the load sits in MEM/WB, so the
late operand is MEM/WB.read_data (a flop, never the dmem DO), or the
carried pre-load value if the load trapped (MEM/WB.ctrl.reg_write = 0).
A 32-bit eq / lt / ltu on two flop-fed operands, ANDed with the lf_*
flags, gives late_redirect; target = EX/MEM.alt_target (flop). A branch
in MEM never has a memory op, so it always advances: late_redirect
fires exactly once. MEM also recomputes branch_taken / pc_next for
MEM/WB (RVFI pc_wdata) and substitutes the late operand into
MEM/WB.rs?_val (RVFI rs?_rdata).

late_redirect has priority over the EX redirect everywhere the EX
redirect acts: PC mux (late ? late_tgt : redirect ? redirect_tgt : ...),
flush_id, loop_buf / fetch_store redirect clears, and additionally
bubbles the EX-stage instruction into EX/MEM (valid + side-effect ctrl
only, as the narrow flush does). A divide in EX is killed through the
existing flush (req drops, divider self-recovers).

Predictor training moves from EX/MEM to MEM/WB flops (add branch_taken
and ctr to mem_wb_t) so late outcomes train correctly; one cycle later
training is harmless (idempotent write).

Timing: the new path is flop -> 32-bit compare -> late_redirect -> PC /
flush / EX/MEM ctrl, the same shape as the existing EX branch resolve
and shorter than the ALU -> ex_result -> forward -> ID/EX loop that
caps Fmax. The risks are one extra input on the PC-mux select and on
flush_id, and the IF-word is_branch term on load_use (it is decoded in
parallel with the rd compares on the same IF-word bits, so it should
fold into the existing load_use LUTs). Area ~ +80-110 LUT, ~ +40 FF.
Expected: ~3.42M cycles (-3.6 to -3.8%); fitness +2 to +4% if median
Fmax holds within ~1%, which is the dominant uncertainty.

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-002-r13s1 (regression, -11.22%): The second try at resolving load -> branch pairs in MEM scored 274.15 vs r11s1's 308.79, almost the same loss as r13s0's 269.85, even though this build fed the late 32-bit eq/lt/ltu compare only from flops (MEM/WB.read_data, the carried operand and alt_target) instead of r13s0's wb_w_data mux. No cycles or Fmax were reported, but fitness ≈ 10 × MHz / Mcycles implies about 94-97 MHz vs 109.53, so the depth of the compare's inputs was not the cause. Both builds shared two things: a same-cycle late_redirect given priority over the EX redirect on the PC mux, flush_id and the loop_buf/fetch_store clears (any_redirect), and the IF-word BRANCH term on load_use. The forecast's "shorter than the ALU loop" argument misses that a higher-priority redirect source likely adds a mux/OR level to the already-tied EX compare -> redirect -> PC/flush_id cone, however short its own path is. This build also added an EX/MEM mem_read/mem_write/valid kill and moved predictor training to MEM/WB. Two same-cycle variants have now each lost 11-13% chasing an interlock worth under 4% of cycles, so on this core a new redirect source must be registered (redirect_mem_q acting one cycle later) or left out.

title: Stride load-address predictor: read a BSRAM dmem shadow one stage early so the hit is a flop in MEM
motivation:
The branch-predictor lever is nearly used up on the r11s1 champion
(308.79, 109.53 MHz, 3.547M cycles). Only ~51k direction mispredicts and
~14k JALRs remain, which is at most ~1.8% even with perfect prediction.
The largest cycle sink left is dmem backpressure. At ~2.9M instructions
there are ~0.6M loads, and each one waits 0.28 cycles on average in MEM
(~170k frozen cycles). r12s1 measured the prize: a 4K-word BSRAM dmem
shadow cut cycles to 3.394M (-4.3%), but it lost Fmax (100 MHz). Its DO
was read at the EX/MEM edge and used in the same MEM cycle, so BSRAM tCO
plus the tag compare drove dmem_stall -> stall_if/stall_id/stall_ex_mem/
hold_mem_wb/flush_id, and the shadow word became a 4th input on the
last-level load-forward mux. LESSONS says this lever is closed "unless
the hit can be decided from flops before MEM". A load-address predictor
does exactly that. It supplies the shadow read address one stage early
from flops only (the PC flop through a small LUT-RAM table, the same
rule that made r11s1's fetch store free). The shadow DO then arrives in
EX, where it is checked against the real AGU address and registered, so
in MEM the hit and the shadow load value are plain flops.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add rtl/load_pred.sv (stride address predictor) and rtl/load_shadow.sv
(BSRAM dmem copy). Keep the IF word, the PC mux, flush_id, the ALU ->
ex_result -> forward loop and the late load_data forward input unchanged.

1. Predictor table (load_pred.sv). 32 entries indexed by the IF PC flop
   pc[6:2], in distributed LUT-RAM (~12 units), with zero init.
   Entry = {v, pidx[13:2], last[13:2]}. Async read from the PC flop only
   (never from the IF word or next_pc). pidx is the predicted word index
   of this PC's next access. Training uses one sync write port driven
   only by EX/MEM flops, for every valid LOAD or STORE in MEM
   (EX/MEM.pc[6:2], mem_addr[13:2], and the carried `last` read at
   predict time):
     stride = a - last; pidx <= a + stride; last <= a; v <= 1.
   The write is idempotent, so a held EX/MEM is harmless. There is no
   tag, because a wrong prediction only costs a miss.
2. Shadow (load_shadow.sv). This is r12s1's arrays reused: a direct-
   mapped 4096-word copy in inferred block_ram, with four 4096x8 byte-lane
   arrays plus a 4096x{valid, tag[3:0]} tag array (index addr[13:2], tag
   addr[17:14]). Only addr[31:18] == 0 is eligible, which excludes MMIO.
   Read address = the table's pidx (PC flop -> LUT-RAM -> BSRAM address,
   with no adder and no IF-word term). It is registered on the ID/EX data
   enable (!stall_id), so while an instruction sits in ID/EX, DO holds the
   predicted entry for it. Register pidx_q and last_q into ID/EX.
   The write port uses MEM-cycle flops and io_dmemRData only (r10s1 rule):
   - a LOAD completing from the bus (dmem_ready, aligned, eligible) fills
     the word and sets {1, tag};
   - a completing STORE writes its byte lanes, and sets {1, tag} if it is
     a full SW or its own registered sh_hit_q was 1 (merge into a held
     word), else {0, x}.
3. Verify in EX (flop and DO in, flop out, off the forward loop):
     sh_hit = mem_read_or_write && v_q && agu_sum[13:2] == pidx_q
              && agu_sum[31:18] == 0 && DO.valid && DO.tag == agu_sum[17:14]
              && aligned && !st_near_q
   st_near_q is a flop set at the ID/EX capture when a STORE was in ID/EX
   or EX/MEM, i.e. one that has not yet written the shadow. It kills
   read-after-write races conservatively.
   sh_val is DO extracted in EX with the same width/sext/agu_sum[1:0]
   decode that already feeds the ld_* pre-decode.
   Register into EX/MEM (!stall enable): sh_hit_q, sh_val_q[31:0],
   wait_op_q = mem_write | (mem_read & !sh_hit), and
   late_ld_q = mem_to_reg & !sh_hit.
4. MEM/hazard, with no new logic level on any tied cone:
   - hazard_unit's ex_mem_mem_op input becomes the wait_op_q flop, so a
     shadow-hit LOAD completes under !dmem_ready (the dmem_stall LUT keeps
     the same inputs).
   - The ID side's mem_is_load becomes late_ld_q (a flop, as before).
   - A hit load's value enters the EARLY forward source:
     fwd_data = alu_or_mul | ({32{sh_hit_q}} & sh_val_q). ID clears the
     add/logic lane selects for LOAD (its alu_result was don't-care) so
     that alu_result = 0 for loads.
   - MEM/WB.read_data <= sh_hit_q ? sh_val_q : load_data, a flop-selected
     mux that sits off the forward loop. The RVFI mem_rdata takes the raw
     shadow word on a hit, and this path is pruned in synthesis.
   The load_data -> rs?_fwd last-level mux, ex_result, the IF word, the
   PC mux and flush_id stay byte-identical to r11s1.

Why it should help: stride/last-address prediction covers stack
reloads (stride 0), globals, the state-machine byte walk (stride 1),

lesson: - 2026-09-29 hyp-20260929-003-r13s2 (placement_failed, n/a): The failure was a synthesis error, not a placement result: GowinSynthesis aborts any loop that runs past 2000 iterations (ERROR EX3934), so the `initial for (i = 0; i < 4096; i++)` zero-fill of load_shadow.sv's 4096-deep lane and tag arrays turned the module into a black box, which then failed P&R. Verilator lint, cosim, cocotb and formal all passed because none of them run the vendor synthesizer, while r11s1's 1024-entry fetch_store loop stays under the limit. Any RAM deeper than 2000 entries must therefore be initialized with $readmemh or with loops of at most 2000 iterations, and the Gowin flow (`make timing`) must be run before handoff. The implementer's Verilator run also sized the prize: 3.514M bracketed CoreMark cycles vs r11s1's ~3.547M (-0.9%, against a -2.5 to -3.1% forecast), and a 128-entry table saved only 0.13% more. No hit count was taken, so the shortfall cannot be split between low stride coverage and the widened sh_near race kills. Even with Fmax held, a PC-indexed stride predictor feeding the dmem shadow is worth under 1% as built, so it should not be retried unless the ISS first shows a much higher shadow-hit rate.

title: Fetch-store re-key (entry K holds word(K+4)) so a predicted-taken transfer reads word(T+4) at pc_imm[11:2], plus fetch-store hits during loop-buffer CAPTURE
motivation:
A fresh `make timing` on the r11s1 champion (place_option 0, 108.2 MHz) shows
the top 25 paths tied within about 1% (9.10-9.21 ns data delay). They cover
about eight separate cones: imm -> adder -> ex_result -> forward -> mul_a_sx
and rs1_val; shamt -> shifter -> forward -> rs2_val; pc -> branch_pred ->
pred/trig -> loop_buf end_q CE; imem_ready -> load_use -> stall_if -> PC CE;
rs1_val -> compare -> redirect -> flush_id -> ID/EX ctrl RESET; IF word ->
imm_gen -> pc+imm -> pre_result; IF word -> regfile -> forward -> rs2_val.
r5s0, r6s0 and r8s0 already showed that cutting one or two of these buys
nothing, so a micro-opt this round has to cut cycles without adding load
or depth to any of these cones.

Nearly all the imem stalls left after r11s1 are the two words fetched
straight from imem after every transfer. The fetch store is read two
fetches ahead from the PC flop, and a predicted-taken advance clears v1_q,
so both word(T) and word(T+4) come from the 22%-stall bus. Each costs
p/(1-p) = 0.28 cycles on average. That happens after about 346k
predicted-taken branches and JALs, except where loop_buf is replaying. Also,
during a loop_buf CAPTURE pass hit_q is forced to 0, so every word of the
first pass through each newly entered loop comes from imem, even when the
fetch store already holds it.
